questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Passage: The Constitution permits preventive detention but surrounds it with safeguards: the detaining authority must communicate the grounds of detention and afford the detenu the earliest opportunity of making a representation (Article 22(5)). A detention order under the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988, does not inform the detenu of his right to make a representation to the Union government against the order. Under the stated principle, the strongest ground to challenge the continued detention is:
o: That the detenu was on bail in a parallel criminal case, which automatically voids any detention order
That the failure to inform the detenu of his right of representation cuts at the root of the Article 22(5) constitutional safeguard and renders the continued detention constitutionally vulnerable
That preventive detention has been declared unconstitutional in all circumstances
That only the detaining officer, and not any higher authority, can consider a representation
questions.e: Article 22(5) guarantees the detenu the earliest opportunity of making a representation; non-communication of the right to represent strikes at the root of the safeguard, as the Karnataka High Court held in September 2026. Bail in a parallel case does not by itself void a detention order.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Passage: The Supreme Court has held in several judgments that determining a person's citizenship is a function of the competent authority under the citizenship law (the Ministry of Home Affairs), not of the Election Commission of India; the Commission's role is to register voters who are citizens. During a Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, the ECI passes an order declaring a group of registered voters to be non-citizens and deleting their names on that ground. Under the stated principle, this order is most vulnerable on the ground that:
o: The ECI has no power to conduct Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls at all
The ECI exceeded its remit: adjudication of citizenship belongs to the competent authority under the citizenship law, not the Election Commission
A voter's name can never be deleted from electoral rolls once registered
The ECI must obtain the Supreme Court's prior permission before every revision
questions.e: The ECI can verify voter eligibility for the rolls, but adjudicating citizenship itself is beyond its constitutional and statutory remit — it is the job of the competent authority under the Citizenship Act, as former SC judge Sudhanshu Dhulia reiterated in September 2026.

questions.subject: Criminal procedure
questions.q: Passage: Courts have held that a compromise between an accused and a complainant is legally distinct from the question of the accused's liberty: grant or refusal of bail must be decided on factors like the nature of the accusations, the stage of proceedings and the conduct of the accused. An undertrial's bail is cancelled solely because he defaulted on a Rs 45-lakh monetary settlement with the complainant, without any finding of misuse of liberty. Under the stated principle, the cancellation is most vulnerable on the ground that:
o: The accused must be released in every case where a settlement exists, whatever its terms
The accused's liberty was made conditional on fulfilling a monetary obligation, although enforceability of the settlement and deprivation of liberty are legally distinct questions
A sessions court can never cancel bail once granted
Monetary settlements between an accused and a complainant are void in criminal cases
questions.e: The Delhi High Court held in September 2026 that the settlement, the payment and the alleged breach of the settlement cannot by themselves be grounds for granting or refusing bail; the bail application must be reconsidered afresh on its own merits.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Passage: Article 141 declares that the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts; Article 142 empowers the Court to pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it. Exercising Article 142 powers, the Supreme Court ordered the re-induction of war widow Priyanka Saxena into the IAF as an expressly one-off order creating no precedent. Under the stated principle, the order's non-precedential character follows because:
o: Orders under Article 142 are administrative, not judicial, acts
Article 142 powers are confined to contempt cases
An order doing complete justice between the parties in a particular cause does not amount to a declaration of law under Article 141 and therefore does not bind other courts as precedent
The Supreme Court cannot pass orders that bind the government
questions.e: Article 142 relief is tailored to complete justice in the specific cause before the Court; it does not declare law for all courts in the way Article 141 declarations do, so the Court can expressly confine such orders to the case at hand.

questions.subject: Statutory law
questions.q: Passage: The Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act, 1991, provides that the religious character of a place of worship as it existed on 15 August 1947 shall continue, and Section 4 bars any suit or legal proceeding seeking to alter that religious character (subject to the Ayodhya exception). A new suit seeks a court-ordered survey of a mosque to gather evidence for changing its religious character. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The survey is permissible because the Act applies only to completed conversions
The suit is barred because a survey directed at altering the religious character as on 15 August 1947 defeats the statutory freeze
The 1991 Act applies only to places of worship in Uttar Pradesh
Section 4 of the Act was repealed by a 2024 Supreme Court order
questions.e: The 1991 Act freezes the religious character of places of worship as it existed on 15 August 1947 and bars suits or proceedings to alter it; a survey aimed at changing that character is barred by Section 4.

questions.subject: Legal profession
questions.q: Passage: In May 2025 the Supreme Court read down the 100-point evaluation system for designating Senior Advocates. Following that, the Delhi High Court notified amended designation rules in September 2026 scrapping the 100-point evaluation by a permanent committee: designation will now be by the full court through consensus or a two-thirds majority vote, with a permanent secretariat headed by a registrar-rank officer compiling candidate data annually. Under the stated principle, a designation validly made under the scrapped points system:
o: Is automatically void in all cases
Must be challenged only before the Supreme Court within 30 days
Is judged under the law as it then stood; the amended rules govern future designations
Can never be revoked even if obtained by fraud
questions.e: Rule changes operate prospectively: designations validly made under the earlier rules are judged by the law as it then stood, while the amended rules apply to future designations.

questions.subject: Torts
questions.q: Passage: The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher imposes strict liability for the escape of dangerous things, subject to exceptions like act of God and the plaintiff's own fault. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India the Supreme Court evolved the stricter rule of absolute liability for enterprises engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activities. A chemical plant using chlorine gas in a densely populated area suffers a gas leak injuring residents, and pleads that it took all reasonable care and that the leak was an accident. Under the stated principle, the plant is liable:
o: Only if negligence is proved, since it took all reasonable care
Not liable, because accidents are an exception to strict liability
Absolutely liable, because enterprises engaged in hazardous activities owe an absolute and non-delegable duty with no exceptions
Liable only to the extent of the insurance cover it held
questions.e: Under M.C. Mehta's absolute-liability rule, an enterprise carrying on a hazardous activity is liable for harm without proof of negligence and without any of the Rylands exceptions; the duty is absolute and non-delegable.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The Supreme Court has held that Articles 14–16 permit the State to classify persons into groups, but the classification must be based on an intelligible differentia and must have a rational nexus with the object of the law. Arbitrary or hostile discrimination is prohibited, while protective discrimination in favour of disadvantaged groups is permissible. A municipality reserved 40% of shop licences for Scheduled Caste entrepreneurs to promote their economic participation. Ram, a general-category applicant denied a licence, challenges the policy. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The policy fails because Ram is treated differently
The policy fails because only the central government may classify
The policy is valid only if Ram is also given a licence
The policy is valid because it is reasonable classification with a rational nexus to economic uplift
questions.e: Intelligible differentia (SC entrepreneurs) with a rational nexus to economic participation makes the classification reasonable, not arbitrary discrimination.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same principle on Article 14 reasonable classification. The State enacts a law banning night-shift work for all women in private factories, claiming safety. An employer argues this is protective discrimination. Under the stated principle, the classification is most vulnerable to challenge on the ground that:
o: The classification rests on a stereotype rather than a real difference relevant to the object, and is hostile discrimination in effect
Only men can work night shifts
The State cannot legislate on labour
Women are not a class at all
questions.e: Blanket bans based on stereotypes lack a rational nexus with a legitimate protective object and amount to hostile discrimination in effect; the Court has favoured safeguards over bans.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same principle on Article 14 reasonable classification. A law grants free legal aid only to prisoners below the poverty line. A wealthy prisoner denied aid challenges it. The State defends the classification. Which application is correct?
o: The classification fails because all prisoners are identically placed
The classification fails because prisoners have no rights
The classification is reasonable because poverty is an intelligible differentia rationally linked to providing aid where need is greatest
The classification must extend to all citizens immediately
questions.e: Poverty is an intelligible differentia and targeting the poor has a rational nexus with the object's purpose; treating unequals equally is itself unequal.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same principle on Article 14 reasonable classification. A State exempts from a professional tax all persons over 70 years of age. A 65-year-old challenges the exemption. Under the principle, the exemption is:
o: Invalid, because taxes must be uniform for everyone
Valid only if all exemptions are removed
Valid, because the elderly form an intelligible class with a rational nexus to the policy of easing their financial burden
Invalid, because age is never a valid basis for classification
questions.e: Age-based classes are permissible when the differentia is intelligible and rationally linked to the law's object, which an exemption for the elderly satisfies.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same principle on Article 14 reasonable classification. A regulation allows only residents of the city to sit for a municipal recruitment exam, excluding equally qualified non-residents. The most likely judicial response is that:
o: The exclusion is valid because all non-residents are a distinct class
The regulation must be struck down for all exams everywhere
The exclusion is arbitrary discrimination because residence here is not rationally linked to fitness for the job
questions.e: While residence may form a class, the classification must have a rational nexus with the object (job fitness); an unjustified exclusion is arbitrary discrimination.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression, but Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions on specified grounds including public order, decency, and defamation. Restrictions must be reasonable and imposed by law on a listed ground. A law criminalises all political criticism of the government as 'undermining confidence'. The law is most likely:
o: Invalid only if enforced against the press
Valid as a reasonable restriction in the interest of public order
Invalid because criticism of government is not among the Article 19(2) grounds and the restriction is not reasonable
Valid because the government may protect its image
questions.e: 'Undermining confidence in the government' is not a listed ground; a blanket ban on political criticism is neither reasonable nor grounded in 19(2).

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same Articles 19(1)(a)/19(2) principle. A law requires a reasonable 7-day prior notice for large public rallies in a congested district. This restriction is most likely:
o: Invalid because only Parliament can restrict speech
Invalid because all restrictions on rallies are banned
Valid because regulation of timing to preserve public order can be reasonable and is imposed by law
questions.e: A time/place regulation imposed by law on the ground of public order that is proportionate is a classic reasonable restriction.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same Articles 19(1)(a)/19(2) principle. A rule bans a journalist from publishing the name of a sexual assault survivor, punishable by fine. The journalist challenges it. The rule is most likely:
o: Valid because the restriction protects decency and privacy under a listed ground and is reasonable
Valid only if the survivor consents to publication
Invalid because privacy is not a fundamental right
Invalid because journalists enjoy absolute immunity
questions.e: Protecting a survivor's identity falls under decency/privacy and the fine-based prohibition is a reasonable, law-imposed restriction.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same Articles 19(1)(a)/19(2) principle. A State order suspends all mobile internet in a district for six months to 'prevent any possible rumours', without review. The order is most likely:
o: Invalid only because it was issued by the State
Valid because internet is not speech
Invalid because a sweeping six-month shutdown is disproportionate and lacks the least-restrictive safeguards required of a reasonable restriction
Valid because prevention of rumours justifies any restriction
questions.e: Reasonable restrictions must be proportionate; an indefinite six-month shutdown without review is a disproportionate response not permitted by 19(2).

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same Articles 19(1)(a)/19(2) principle. A defamation law permits the person defamed to sue, but requires proof that the statement was false and caused harm. A critic calls the law a violation of free speech. The best answer is:
o: The law is invalid because only the State may sue
The law is a reasonable restriction because defamation is a listed ground and liability turns on falsity and harm, not on mere disagreement
The law is invalid because all criticism is protected
The law applies only to spoken words
questions.e: Defamation is expressly a listed ground, and a law requiring falsity plus harm is narrowly tailored, hence reasonable.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 21 protects life and personal liberty; no person may be deprived of it except by a procedure established by law, which the Supreme Court requires to be fair, just and reasonable rather than arbitrary. A municipal order allows demolition of a person's home within two hours of notice, with no hearing and no appeal. The order is most likely:
o: Invalid because a two-hour notice with no hearing or appeal is an arbitrary procedure violating Article 21
Valid because demolition is not a deprivation of liberty
Invalid only if the house is rented
Valid because the municipality owns the land
questions.e: Article 21 demands a fair, just and reasonable procedure; a summary two-hour demolition without hearing or appeal is arbitrary and fails that test.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same Article 21 principle. A law requires every accused person to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest and allows legal representation. This procedure is most likely:
o: Valid because it is a fair procedure giving prompt judicial oversight and access to counsel
Invalid because accused persons have no rights
Invalid because 24 hours is too long
questions.e: Prompt production and legal representation are hallmarks of a fair procedure, so the requirement satisfies Article 21's standard.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same Article 21 principle. A statute permits preventive detention for 12 months with the detainee never told the grounds and never allowed to challenge the order. This detention regime is most likely:
o: Valid because preventive detention is completely outside Article 21
Invalid because denying the grounds and any review makes the procedure arbitrary, not fair
Invalid only if the detainee is a citizen
Valid because detention itself proves guilt
questions.e: Even for preventive detention, Article 21 requires a fair procedure; concealing grounds and barring all review is arbitrary.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same Article 21 principle. A prison rule denies all under-trial prisoners any medical care during an epidemic. The most likely judicial response is that:
o: The rule is valid during epidemics
The rule violates Article 21 because denying medical care is an arbitrary deprivation of the right to life, which prisoners retain
The rule only violates the rights of convicts
The rule is valid because prisoners lose all rights
questions.e: Prisoners retain the right to life; arbitrarily denying medical care during an epidemic is not a fair procedure and violates Article 21.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same Article 21 principle. A law requiring fair hearings before licence cancellation also gives the affected person a reasoned order and a right to appeal. This framework is most likely:
o: Invalid because appeal rights slow administration
Invalid because licences are privileges, not rights
Valid because notice, hearing, reasons and appeal together constitute a fair, just and reasonable procedure
questions.e: Notice, hearing, reasoned orders and appeal are the core ingredients of procedural fairness under Article 21.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The Constitution provides five writs. Habeas corpus directs that a detained person be produced before the court; mandamus commands a public authority to perform a legal duty; prohibition restrains a lower authority from acting beyond its jurisdiction; certiorari quashes such an order after it is passed; quo warranto questions the authority by which a person holds public office. A man is picked up by the police and held for a week without being produced before any magistrate. The appropriate writ is:
questions.e: Habeas corpus is the writ that secures production of a person held in custody and tests the legality of detention.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same writs principle. A licensing authority refuses, without reasons, to issue a licence to an applicant who meets every stated statutory condition. The authority has a legal duty to decide applications in accordance with the statute. The appropriate writ is:
questions.e: Mandamus commands a public authority to perform its legal duty; the authority must decide per the statute rather than sit on the application.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same writs principle. A village panchayat committee begins hearing a property-tax dispute that the statute assigns exclusively to the district tribunal. No order has yet been passed. The appropriate writ is:
questions.e: Prohibition restrains a lower body from proceeding in a matter beyond its jurisdiction before it passes an order.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same writs principle. A university disciplinary board, acting beyond the powers given by its statute, expels a student; the expulsion order has already been issued. The appropriate writ is:
questions.e: Certiorari quashes an order already passed by a lower body that acted in excess of its jurisdiction.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same writs principle. A person with no statutory eligibility is sworn in as a municipal councillor. A voter challenges the appointment. The appropriate writ is:
questions.e: Quo warranto asks by what authority a person holds public office and can oust an ineligible occupant.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Negligence requires four elements: a duty of care owed to the claimant, breach of that duty, causation linking the breach to the loss, and damage. A municipal corporation leaves an open manhole on a busy footpath unmarked. A pedestrian looking at the road ahead falls in and is injured. Which element is most clearly satisfied by the unmarked open manhole?
o: Breach of the duty to keep public paths reasonably safe
No element, because the pedestrian should have looked down
questions.e: A municipality owes pedestrians care over footpaths; an open, unmarked manhole is a clear breach of that duty, with causation and damage also evident on these facts.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same negligence principle. A lifeguard at a public pool scrolls on a phone for twenty minutes while a swimmer, struggling in plain view, drowns. The lifeguard's estate argues there was no contract with the swimmer. The best answer is:
o: A duty of care exists from the lifeguard's role, and the inattention is a breach causing the death
Lifeguards owe duties only to children
The swimmer assumed all risk by entering the pool
No duty exists without a contract
questions.e: Duty arises from the lifeguard's role and proximity, not a contract; ignoring a plainly visible struggling swimmer breaches it and causes the death.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same negligence principle. A driver carefully stops at a red light. Seconds later, an earthquake collapses a building onto the car, injuring the driver. A bystander claims the driver was negligent. The claim fails on which element?
o: Duty, because drivers owe no duty
Breach, because careful driving at a red light is not careless conduct
questions.e: Negligence needs breach; stopping correctly at the light is not a breach, and the earthquake is not the driver's carelessness.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Defamation requires a false statement of fact, publication to a third party, and harm to reputation. A blogger writes that a restaurant owner 'poisons customers', knowing inspections found no such thing; readers cancel bookings. Which element is NOT satisfied?
o: Falsity, because inspections contradict the claim
All elements are satisfied, so none is missing
questions.e: Falsity, publication to readers, and reputational harm (lost bookings) are all present; no element is missing.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same defamation principle. In a private diary never shown to anyone, a woman writes that her neighbour is 'a thief'. The neighbour finds the diary. He sues for defamation. The claim fails because:
o: The diary is protected by copyright
There was no publication to a third party
questions.e: Defamation requires communication to a third party; a private diary entry read only by the writer was never published.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: A valid contract generally requires offer, acceptance, lawful consideration, capacity, free consent and a lawful object. A 15-year-old signs an agreement to buy a laptop on credit, paying monthly instalments. When sued for default, the minor's best defence is:
o: The minor lacks contractual capacity, so the agreement is void
The shop should have asked for cash
questions.e: Minors lack capacity to contract; agreements with minors are void (except for necessaries), so the credit agreement is unenforceable.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same contract principle. A shopkeeper puts a 'sale: 50% off all shirts' board outside. A customer demands a shirt at half price; the shopkeeper refuses to sell. Under the principle, the board is most likely:
o: An offer that the shopkeeper must honour
An invitation to offer; the customer makes the offer by asking to buy
An acceptance of the customer's standing offer
questions.e: Advertisements and display boards are generally invitations to offer; the customer offers by presenting the goods for purchase, which the shopkeeper may accept or refuse.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same contract principle. Under threat of having his shop demolished, a trader signs a supply agreement he would never otherwise accept. He later seeks to avoid it. The agreement is vulnerable because:
o: Consent was obtained by coercion and was not free
The supplier had more bargaining power
questions.e: Coercion vitiates free consent; a contract induced by threats is voidable at the option of the coerced party.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same contract principle. Two parties agree that one will pay the other to destroy a rival's warehouse. The 'contract' is:
o: Valid because both parties consented freely
Void because its object is unlawful
Voidable only by the party who pays
questions.e: An agreement with an unlawful object (arson/destruction of property) is void; free consent cannot cure an illegal object.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Consideration must be lawful and must move at the promisor's desire, though it need not be adequate. A promises B ₹5,000 in gratitude for past voluntary help B gave. Later A refuses to pay. B sues. The claim is most likely to fail because:
o: Past voluntary service is not consideration at the promisor's desire, so there is no binding contract
B should have asked for more
questions.e: Consideration must move at the promisor's desire; a promise in return for past voluntary acts generally lacks valid consideration.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: An employer is vicariously liable for a tort committed by an employee acting in the course of employment, even without personal fault. A delivery driver, rushing to complete a company delivery, runs a red light and injures a pedestrian. The company argues it told drivers to obey traffic rules. The company is:
o: Liable only if the driver is bankrupt
Not liable because it gave proper instructions
Liable because the driver was acting in the course of employment when the tort occurred
Not liable because driving is the driver's personal act
questions.e: Instructions do not defeat vicarious liability; the tort was committed while performing the employer's work, so the company answers for it.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same vicarious liability principle. An accountant, on a personal holiday, crashes his own car while shopping for groceries. His employer is sued. The employer is:
o: Not liable because the act had no connection with the course of employment
Liable because all employees bind their employers
Not liable because accountants are professionals
questions.e: Vicarious liability needs the tort to be in the course of employment; a holiday grocery trip in a personal car is outside it.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Strict liability (Rylands v Fletcher) makes a person liable for harm escaping from a dangerous thing kept on their land, even without negligence, subject to exceptions like act of God. A factory stores large quantities of toxic chemicals; the tank, though properly maintained, develops an unforeseeable defect and leaks into a neighbour's well. The factory is:
o: Not liable because the defect was unforeseeable
Liable only if the neighbour complained earlier
Liable under strict liability because a dangerous thing escaped and caused harm, and proper maintenance is no defence
Not liable because it maintained the tank properly
questions.e: Strict liability does not require negligence; escape of a dangerous substance causing harm triggers liability, with only narrow exceptions.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same strict liability principle. A farmer keeps a domesticated cow that breaks through a fence during an unprecedented flood and damages a neighbour's crop. The farmer's best defence is:
o: Act of God, because the unprecedented flood is a natural extraordinary event beyond control
The neighbour should have built a wall
questions.e: Act of God is a recognised exception to strict liability where an extraordinary natural event, not the keeper's conduct, caused the escape.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Volenti non fit injuria: one who voluntarily accepts a known risk cannot later claim for injury within that risk. A spectator at a cricket match sits in an unscreened area despite warnings, and is hit by a six. The spectator sues the stadium. The stadium's best defence is:
o: Volenti non fit injuria, because the spectator knowingly accepted the ordinary risk of the game
questions.e: Sitting in an unscreened area with knowledge of the game's ordinary risks amounts to voluntary assumption of that risk.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A confession made to a police officer is inadmissible in evidence. However, information leading to discovery of a fact may be proved. An accused tells a police officer, 'I buried the knife behind the shed', and the knife is recovered there. What is admissible?
o: The statement only if the accused repeats it in court
The entire confession including the statement
Only the fact of discovery of the knife consequent on the information, not the confession itself
Nothing at all may be proved
questions.e: Confessions to police are inadmissible, but the discovery of the fact (the knife) pursuant to the information is admissible under the discovery exception.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: No person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. An accused is forced by police to sign a written confession. In court, the prosecution seeks to rely on it. The confession is:
o: Admissible because it is in writing
Inadmissible because it was compelled, violating the privilege against self-incrimination
Admissible if the judge finds it true
Inadmissible only if the accused is innocent
questions.e: Article 20(3) protects against compelled self-incrimination; a confession extracted by compulsion cannot be used against the accused.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Double jeopardy — no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. A person is tried and acquitted of theft on merits. The State files a fresh prosecution for the same theft on the same facts. The second prosecution is:
o: Valid because the first ended in acquittal
Barred by double jeopardy under Article 20(2)
Valid if new evidence is found
Barred only if the punishment is severe
questions.e: Article 20(2) bars a second prosecution and punishment for the same offence after a trial on merits; acquittal triggers the protection.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Ex post facto — no person shall be convicted for an act that was not an offence when done, nor given a greater penalty than applied then. A new law in 2026 criminalises an act done in 2024 and prescribes 5 years' imprisonment. Prosecuting the 2024 act under the 2026 law is:
o: Valid because the act is now criminal
Barred by Article 20(1), which prohibits retrospective criminalisation
Valid if the penalty is reduced
questions.e: Article 20(1) prohibits convicting a person under a law that did not make the act an offence when committed.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: An offer lapses if not accepted within the stipulated or a reasonable time. A offers to sell his car to B, 'offer open till Monday'. B accepts on Wednesday. There is:
o: A contract only if A agrees again
A binding contract because B accepted
A voidable contract at B's option
No contract because the offer had lapsed after Monday
questions.e: An offer open till Monday lapses after Monday; acceptance on Wednesday is too late and cannot create a contract.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Acceptance must be communicated to the offeror. B posts a letter of acceptance, which is lost in transit and never reaches A. A, unaware, sells to another. Under the postal rule, where the offeror has authorised post as the mode, the contract is:
o: Complete when B posted the letter
Complete when A reads the letter
Complete only if B sends a second letter
questions.e: Under the postal rule, acceptance is complete as against the offeror when the letter is posted, provided post was an authorised mode.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A counter-offer terminates the original offer. A offers to sell for ₹1,00,000. B replies, 'I will pay ₹80,000.' A refuses. B then says, 'I accept ₹1,00,000.' The legal position is:
o: A contract exists at ₹90,000 as a compromise
No contract, because B's counter-offer killed the original offer
questions.e: A counter-offer terminates the original offer; B cannot later revive the ₹1,00,000 offer by purporting to accept it.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The doctrine of indoor management protects outsiders dealing with a company who rely on its apparent authority, unless they knew of an internal irregularity. A supplier delivers goods to a company's manager, who the board had secretly forbidden from placing orders, a fact the supplier could not have known. The company must pay because:
o: The supplier should have checked the board minutes
The indoor management rule protects the outsider who dealt in good faith without knowledge of the internal restriction
questions.e: Outsiders are entitled to assume internal procedures were followed; a secret board restriction unknown to the supplier cannot defeat the contract.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A child born during a valid marriage is conclusively presumed legitimate unless non-access is proved. In a paternity dispute, the husband proves he was posted abroad for the entire period when conception must have occurred. The presumption is:
o: Rebutted only by a DNA test
questions.e: The conclusive presumption of legitimacy yields to proof of non-access between the spouses during the relevant period.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Res ipsa loquitur allows negligence to be inferred where the accident would not ordinarily occur without negligence and the thing was under the defendant's control. A barrel of flour falls from a warehouse window onto a pedestrian. The pedestrian need not prove the precise negligent act because:
o: Pedestrians can never be at fault
The event speaks for itself: barrels do not fall from windows without negligence, and the warehouse controlled the premises
questions.e: Res ipsa loquitur applies where the accident is of a kind that ordinarily implies negligence and the instrumentality was in the defendant's control.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: In nuisance, the test is reasonableness of the interference judged by locality and duration. A printing press runs noisy machines all night in a purely residential colony. A resident sues. The press's defence that it holds a valid business licence is:
o: Conclusive, because licences authorise all operations
Irrelevant to nuisance, because a licence does not authorise unreasonable interference with neighbours
questions.e: A licence to run a business does not license committing a nuisance; night-long noise in a residential area is an unreasonable interference.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Consent obtained by fraud vitiates consent. A seller shows a buyer a ring, claiming it is diamond, knowing it is glass; the buyer pays the diamond price. The buyer may:
o: Avoid the contract because consent was obtained by fraud
Keep the ring and claim it is diamond
Sue only for the difference in metal value
Do nothing, because he inspected the ring
questions.e: Fraud as to the essential character of the thing sold makes the contract voidable at the defrauded party's option.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A wagering agreement is void. Two friends bet ₹10,000 on an election result, each depositing the sum with a stakeholder. The loser demands the stake back from the stakeholder before it is paid to the winner. The loser:
o: Must share the stake with the winner
Cannot recover because betting debts are honoured
Can recover only after the winner is paid
Can recover the deposit from the stakeholder before payment, since the agreement is void
questions.e: A wagering agreement is void, and money deposited with a stakeholder may be recovered before it is paid over to the winner.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: An agreement in restraint of trade is void, except a reasonable restraint on sale of goodwill. A retiring partner agrees never to open a competing clinic anywhere in India. The restraint is:
o: Void as an unreasonable restraint of trade
Valid because clinics are essential services
questions.e: A nation-wide lifetime ban on competing is an unreasonable restraint of trade and void; only reasonable restraints ancillary to goodwill sales are saved.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Time is of the essence only where the contract so provides or the nature demands. A contract for sale of land fixes no date for completion. The buyer delays six months. The seller claims breach for delay alone. The claim fails because:
o: The seller should have cancelled earlier
Time was not of the essence, so delay alone is not breach; performance must occur within a reasonable time
questions.e: Unless time is made of the essence, a party must perform within a reasonable time; mere delay without such a term is not itself breach.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A bailee must take as much care of bailed goods as a person of ordinary prudence would take of their own goods. A friend leaves a laptop with another friend, who leaves it on an open balcony during a dust storm. The laptop is damaged. The friend is liable because:
o: Friends are always liable to each other
The standard of an ordinarily prudent person was breached by leaving it exposed in a dust storm
questions.e: Even gratuitous bailees must exercise ordinary prudence; leaving a laptop on an open balcony in a dust storm falls below that standard.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A guarantee requires a principal debtor, a creditor and a surety; the surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor's unless otherwise agreed. A surety guarantees a ₹2,00,000 loan. The borrower defaults. The creditor sues the surety directly without suing the borrower. The suit is:
o: Maintainable only for half the amount
Maintainable because the surety's liability is co-extensive with the borrower's
Not maintainable until the borrower is sued
questions.e: The surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor's, so the creditor may proceed directly against the surety.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Agency: an agent acting within actual or apparent authority binds the principal. A company's purchase manager, authorised to buy office supplies up to ₹50,000, orders machinery worth ₹5,00,000 from a supplier who knew of the limit. The company is:
o: Bound because the manager is its employee
Not bound because the manager exceeded actual authority and the supplier knew of the limit
questions.e: An agent's act beyond actual authority does not bind the principal where the third party knew of the limitation; apparent authority fails on knowledge.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Mistake of fact going to the root may void an agreement; mistake of law does not. Two parties contract for a cargo ship that, unknown to both, had sunk the previous day. The contract is:
o: Valid because both parties were careful
Valid if the price is reduced
Void because of a mutual mistake as to the existence of the subject matter
questions.e: A mutual mistake about the existence of the subject matter goes to the root and renders the agreement void.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Undue influence exists where one party dominates the will of another and obtains an unfair advantage. A spiritual guru persuades an elderly devotee to gift him her house. The gift is vulnerable because:
o: The fiduciary-like dominance raises a presumption of undue influence, shifting the burden to the guru to prove free consent
Gifts to gurus are always void
questions.e: Relationships of spiritual dominance attract the presumption of undue influence; the stronger party must prove the transaction was the free act of the weaker.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution guarantees equality before law and equal protection of the laws?
questions.e: Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of the laws; Articles 15 and 16 are specific applications of it.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The right to constitutional remedies, which Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution, is guaranteed by:
questions.e: Article 32 gives the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights; Ambedkar called it the heart and soul.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Under Article 21, the phrase 'procedure established by law' was interpreted in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) to mean the procedure must be:
questions.e: Maneka Gandhi held that procedure under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable, not merely enacted by the legislature.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The Basic Structure doctrine, holding that Parliament cannot amend the Constitution's essential features, was laid down in:
o: Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
SR Bommai v. Union of India
questions.e: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) propounded the basic structure doctrine limiting Parliament's amending power under Article 368.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Which writ is issued to a lower court or tribunal to transfer a case or quash its order for exceeding jurisdiction?
questions.e: Certiorari is issued by a superior court to quash the order of a lower court or tribunal acting without or in excess of jurisdiction.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added which words to the Preamble?
questions.e: The 42nd Amendment inserted 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' into the Preamble during the Emergency.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 44th Amendment (1978) removed which of the following from the list of fundamental rights?
questions.e: The 44th Amendment deleted the right to property from Part III, making it a legal right under Article 300A.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Right to property is now protected as a constitutional right under:
questions.e: After the 44th Amendment, the right to property survives as a constitutional (legal) right under Article 300A, not a fundamental right.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in which Part of the Constitution?
questions.e: Directive Principles are in Part IV (Articles 36–51); Part IVA contains fundamental duties.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Fundamental duties were added to the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment in:
questions.e: The 42nd Amendment inserted Part IVA with Article 51A listing the fundamental duties.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Which Schedule of the Constitution contains the official languages recognised by the Constitution?
questions.e: The Eighth Schedule lists the 22 officially recognised languages; the Seventh distributes legislative subjects.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment, deals with:
questions.e: The Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985) contains the anti-defection law disqualifying legislators who defect.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The distribution of legislative powers between the Union and States is found in:
questions.e: The Seventh Schedule contains the Union, State and Concurrent Lists allocating legislative subjects.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Education was moved from the State List to the Concurrent List by the:
questions.e: The 42nd Amendment (1976) transferred education (and forests, weights and measures, etc.) to the Concurrent List.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 73rd Amendment (1992) is associated with:
questions.e: The 73rd Amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions (Part IX, Eleventh Schedule).

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 74th Amendment (1992) is associated with:
questions.e: The 74th Amendment constitutionalised urban local bodies — municipalities, municipal councils and corporations (Part IXA).

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced:
questions.e: The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced the Goods and Services Tax, creating Article 246A and the GST Council.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 103rd Amendment (2019) provides for:
questions.e: The 103rd Amendment inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6) enabling 10% EWS reservation in education and public employment.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 86th Amendment (2002) made elementary education a fundamental right under:
questions.e: The 86th Amendment inserted Article 21A guaranteeing free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 61st Amendment (1988) is known for:
o: Lowering the voting age from 21 to 18
questions.e: The 61st Amendment amended Article 326, reducing the voting age from 21 to 18 years.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Which Article empowers the President to impose President's Rule in a State?
questions.e: Article 356 allows President's Rule on the failure of constitutional machinery in a State; Article 352 is the national emergency.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Financial Emergency is provided for in:
questions.e: Article 360 provides for a Financial Emergency; it has never been proclaimed in India.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The power of judicial review of legislative action flows primarily from:
questions.e: Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with fundamental rights void, anchoring judicial review of legislation.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In SR Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that:
o: Preamble is not part of the Constitution
Secularism is part of the basic structure and President's Rule is subject to judicial review
questions.e: SR Bommai held secularism to be part of the basic structure and made proclamations under Article 356 subject to judicial review.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The collegium system for appointment of judges was established through:
o: The Second and Third Judges cases interpreting Article 124
questions.e: The Second (1993) and Third (1998) Judges cases created the collegium system, giving primacy to the Chief Justice of India and senior judges.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The National Judicial Appointments Commission Act was struck down in 2015 in:
o: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (Fourth Judges case)
questions.e: The Fourth Judges case (2015) struck down the NJAC as violating the independence of the judiciary, part of the basic structure.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The minimum age for election as President of India is:
questions.e: Article 58 requires the President to be at least 35 years old, qualified for Lok Sabha election, and not holding an office of profit.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The Vice-President of India is elected by:
o: Members of both Houses of Parliament (elected and nominated)
An electoral college of all MLAs and MPs
questions.e: Under Article 66, the Vice-President is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament, including nominated members.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Money Bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha under:
questions.e: Article 110 defines a Money Bill and Article 109 gives the special procedure: introduction only in the Lok Sabha.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 'doctrine of eclipse' in Indian constitutional law holds that:
o: A pre-constitutional law inconsistent with fundamental rights is eclipsed (inoperative) but revives if the inconsistency is removed
A law violating fundamental rights is dead forever
questions.e: Under the doctrine of eclipse (Bhikaji Narain), an inconsistent pre-constitutional law is overshadowed, not obliterated, and revives if the defect is cured.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 'doctrine of severability' under Article 13 means:
o: The Constitution can be severed into parts
States can sever ties with the Union
Only the offending part of a law is void, and the valid part survives if severable
questions.e: Severability allows courts to strike down only the unconstitutional portion of a law while preserving the valid remainder.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 'doctrine of pith and substance' is used to resolve:
o: Whether a law falls within the legislature's competence under the Seventh Schedule lists
questions.e: Pith and substance examines a law's true nature to decide which legislative list it belongs to when lists appear to overlap.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 'doctrine of colourable legislation' applies when:
o: A legislature does indirectly what it cannot do directly, exceeding its competence
A law is printed in colour
questions.e: Colourable legislation is the doctrine that a legislature cannot do indirectly what the Constitution forbids it to do directly.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 'doctrine of harmonious construction' requires courts to:
o: Strike down one of two conflicting provisions
Read provisions so as to give effect to both as far as possible
questions.e: Harmonious construction holds that provisions of the Constitution or a statute should be read together so each retains effect.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 'doctrine of territorial nexus' in Article 245 relates to:
o: Parliament's power to legislate for extra-territorial operations
A State legislature's power to make laws with extra-territorial effect if there is a sufficient nexus with the State
The territory of Jammu and Kashmir
questions.e: A State law may have extra-territorial operation if there is a sufficient territorial nexus between the State and the object of the law.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The 'doctrine of legitimate expectation' in administrative law protects:
o: A person's reasonable expectation arising from a promise or past practice, requiring fair procedure before it is denied
questions.e: Legitimate expectation requires public authorities to act fairly — usually by giving a hearing — before defeating an expectation they created.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Which case established the 'rarest of rare' doctrine for the death penalty in India?
o: Jagmohan Singh v. State of U.P.
Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
Both Bachan Singh and Machhi Singh elaborated it
Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab
questions.e: Bachan Singh (1980) laid down the 'rarest of rare' standard; Machhi Singh (1983) elaborated guidelines for applying it.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), the Supreme Court:
o: Laid down guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace
questions.e: Vishaka guidelines on workplace sexual harassment filled the legislative vacuum until the 2013 Act was passed.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The Right to Information Act was enacted in the year:
questions.e: The RTI Act, 2005 operationalised the citizen's right to seek information from public authorities, flowing from Article 19(1)(a).

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Under Article 15, the State may make special provisions for women and children under clause:
questions.e: Article 15(3) expressly permits special provisions for women and children, an exception to the non-discrimination rule.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Actus reus' refers to:
o: The guilty act or prohibited conduct
questions.e: Actus reus is the physical, prohibited act element of a crime, paired with mens rea (the mental element).

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Audi alteram partem' means:
o: The king can do no wrong
No one is above the law
questions.e: Audi alteram partem — hear the other side — is a core principle of natural justice requiring a fair hearing.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Caveat emptor' means:
questions.e: Caveat emptor places the duty of inspection on the buyer; the seller need not disclose defects the buyer could discover.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Res judicata' means:
o: A thing decided; a matter already adjudicated cannot be re-litigated between the same parties
questions.e: Res judicata bars re-litigation of a matter finally decided between the same parties on the same cause of action.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Sub judice' refers to a matter:
o: Under judicial consideration and therefore not to be publicly prejudged
questions.e: Sub judice describes a matter pending before a court, which should not be publicly discussed in ways that prejudice it.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Ex parte' describes proceedings:
o: With only one party present or on behalf of one party
questions.e: Ex parte means on behalf of or involving only one side, such as an urgent interim order heard without the other party.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Prima facie' means:
o: At first sight; sufficient to establish a case unless rebutted
questions.e: Prima facie denotes evidence that, at first sight, is enough to prove a case unless contradicted or explained.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Bona fide' means:
questions.e: Bona fide means in good faith, honestly and without fraud or deception.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Mala fide' means:
questions.e: Mala fide means in bad faith — with dishonest or improper motive, the opposite of bona fide.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Nemo judex in causa sua' means:
o: No one should be a judge in their own cause
Ignorance of law is no excuse
questions.e: Nemo judex in causa sua is the natural-justice rule against bias: no one may judge a case in which they are interested.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Ignorantia juris non excusat' means:
o: Ignorance of fact is no excuse
Ignorance of law is no excuse
questions.e: Ignorantia juris non excusat — not knowing the law does not excuse its breach, though mistake of fact may.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Volenti non fit injuria' means:
o: To one who is willing, no harm is done (legally)
questions.e: Volenti non fit injuria is the defence that one who voluntarily accepts a known risk cannot claim for resulting injury.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Res ipsa loquitur' is best translated as:
questions.e: Res ipsa loquitur — the thing speaks for itself — lets negligence be inferred from the nature of the accident.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Ubi jus ibi remedium' means:
o: Where there is a right, there is a remedy
questions.e: Ubi jus ibi remedium expresses that every legal right has a corresponding legal remedy for its violation.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Damnum sine injuria' refers to:
o: Loss without violation of a legal right, giving no cause of action
questions.e: Damnum sine injuria is loss suffered without infringement of a legal right — e.g., lawful competition — so no action lies.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Injuria sine damno' refers to:
o: Violation of a legal right without actual damage, which is still actionable
questions.e: Injuria sine damno is infringement of a legal right (like trespass) that is actionable even without measurable loss.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Stare decisis' means:
o: Let the decision stand; follow precedent
The court must stare at evidence
questions.e: Stare decisis is the doctrine of precedent: courts follow earlier binding decisions on the same point of law.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Obiter dicta' refers to:
o: A judge's incidental remarks not essential to the decision, which are persuasive but not binding
The binding part of a judgment
questions.e: Obiter dicta are observations made in passing; only the ratio decidendi (the reason for the decision) binds.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Ratio decidendi' means:
o: The reason for the decision; the binding legal principle of a case
questions.e: Ratio decidendi is the legal reasoning necessary to the decision, which forms the binding precedent.

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'De novo' trial means:
o: A trial with new judges only
A trial afresh from the beginning
questions.e: De novo means anew; a de novo trial or hearing starts from the beginning rather than continuing the earlier proceeding.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: In 2024, the Supreme Court in the electoral bonds case (Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India) held the Electoral Bond Scheme:
o: Unconstitutional, violating the right to information under Article 19(1)(a)
questions.e: The Court struck down the scheme as unconstitutional, holding anonymous political funding violates voters' right to information.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The three new criminal laws replacing the IPC, CrPC and Indian Evidence Act came into force on:
questions.e: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam came into force on 1 July 2024.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the offence of sedition (Section 124A IPC) has been replaced by:
o: Section 150 BNS dealing with acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity
questions.e: BNS Section 150 punishes acts endangering India's sovereignty, unity and integrity — the reworked successor to the sedition provision.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, which received assent in 2023, primarily governs:
o: Processing of digital personal data and the rights of data principals
questions.e: The DPDP Act, 2023 regulates processing of digital personal data, consent, and rights of data principals, enforced by a Data Protection Board.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: In 2023, the Supreme Court's Constitution Bench in Supriyo v. Union of India held regarding same-sex marriage that:
o: There is no fundamental right to marry for same-sex couples; legalisation is for Parliament
The Special Marriage Act already covers it
Adoption rights were granted to same-sex couples
Same-sex couples have a fundamental right to marry
questions.e: The majority held there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry and left legal recognition of same-sex marriage to the legislature.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Women's Reservation Act (106th Amendment, 2023) reserves:
o: 33% of seats in Lok Sabha and State assemblies for women
questions.e: The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State legislative assemblies for women, effective after delimitation.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: Article 370 was abrogated in August 2019; in December 2023 the Supreme Court in Re: Article 370 held that:
o: Statehood must be restored within 30 days
The abrogation was valid and J&K has no internal sovereignty distinct from other States
questions.e: The Constitution Bench unanimously upheld the abrogation, holding J&K had no internal sovereignty and Article 370 was temporary.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Waqf (Amendment) Act passed by Parliament in 2025 was challenged on the ground that it violated:
o: Articles 14, 25 and 26 concerning equality and religious freedom
questions.e: Petitions argued the amendments infringed equality and the freedom to manage religious affairs under Articles 14, 25 and 26 (reported litigation, 2025).

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: In 2024, the Supreme Court ruled that States have the power to levy tax on mineral rights, holding in Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India that:
o: The Mines and Minerals Act is void
Royalty is not a tax, and States may levy tax on mineral-bearing lands
questions.e: The 9-judge Bench held royalty is not a tax and States can tax mineral rights under their legislative entries.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Supreme Court's 2024 ruling on sub-classification of Scheduled Castes (State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh) held that:
o: Creamy layer applies to SCs automatically
States may sub-classify SCs/STs for reservation to benefit the most disadvantaged, with quantifiable data
questions.e: The 7-judge Bench overruled E.V. Chinnaiah, permitting States to sub-classify SCs based on quantifiable data on backwardness.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) replaced which law?
questions.e: BNSS replaced the CrPC; BNS replaced the IPC and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam replaced the Evidence Act.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: Zero FIR, allowing an FIR to be registered at any police station regardless of jurisdiction, is provided under:
o: BNSS provisions carried forward from CrPC practice and now codified
questions.e: Zero FIR practice is codified under the BNSS (Section 173), requiring registration irrespective of territorial jurisdiction.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: In 2025, the Supreme Court held in the 'bulldozer justice' matter that demolitions as punishment without due process violate:
o: Article 21 and the rule of law; guidelines were issued requiring notice and hearing
questions.e: The Court condemned punitive demolitions without due process and laid down pan-India guidelines including show-cause notice and hearing (2024–25 litigation).

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Mediation Act, 2023 in India:
o: Provides a statutory framework for mediation including mandatory pre-litigation mediation in certain civil disputes
Makes pre-litigation mediation voluntary in all cases
questions.e: The Mediation Act, 2023 institutionalises mediation with provisions including mandatory pre-litigation mediation for specified civil/commercial disputes.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: In the 2024 Chandigarh mayoral election case, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to:
o: Declare the defeated candidate the winner after finding ballot tampering by the presiding officer
Transfer the case to the High Court
questions.e: Finding the returning officer defaced ballots, the Court used Article 142 to declare the rightful winner, calling it a murder of democracy.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Supreme Court's 2026 ruling on the 'right to be forgotten' debate (approximate; area of evolving law) is best described as:
o: An evolving area where courts balance privacy under Article 21 against free speech and public interest case-by-case
questions.e: Indian courts have recognised the right to be forgotten as flowing from privacy but apply it case-by-case against competing speech and public-interest claims; label: evolving law.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 introduced which new concept for misleading advertisements?
o: Central Consumer Protection Authority with power against misleading ads and endorsements
questions.e: The 2019 Act created the CCPA, which can act against misleading advertisements and hold endorsers liable for due-diligence failures.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: Euthanasia in India: the Supreme Court in Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) held that:
o: Passive euthanasia and advance medical directives ('living wills') are permissible under Article 21
questions.e: Common Cause recognised the right to die with dignity, permitting passive euthanasia and advance directives subject to safeguards.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act, 1991, frequently litigated in recent years, provides that:
o: Only the Ayodhya site is covered
The religious character of places of worship as on 15 August 1947 shall be maintained
New temples may not be built
All religious sites vest in the State
questions.e: The 1991 Act freezes the religious character of places of worship as it existed on 15 August 1947, barring suits to alter it (Ayodhya excepted).

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: In 2023–24, the Supreme Court's ruling on the appointment of Election Commissioners (Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India) led to:
o: A 2023 Act creating a selection committee of the PM, a Union Minister and the Leader of Opposition
questions.e: After Anoop Baranwal suggested a committee including the CJI, Parliament's 2023 Act set up a panel of the PM, a Cabinet Minister and the LoP.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: 'Digitisation promised to democratise access to courts. Filing moved online, cause lists became searchable, and judgments appeared within hours. Yet the same transformation quietly erected a new barrier: the litigant who cannot navigate a portal, afford stable connectivity, or read English is now doubly disadvantaged — once by the dispute, and again by the medium. Technology, the great leveller in theory, can entrench exclusion in practice unless design begins with the least connected user.' The author's primary concern is that:
o: English should be banned in courts
Digital reforms may deepen exclusion unless designed for the least connected
questions.e: The passage argues digitisation helps but can entrench exclusion; the concern is design that ignores the least connected user.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same digitisation passage. The phrase 'doubly disadvantaged' refers to:
o: Being disadvantaged by the dispute and again by the digital medium
questions.e: The text explicitly defines it: once by the dispute, and again by the medium.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same digitisation passage. The author's tone is best described as:
questions.e: The author acknowledges benefits but warns of exclusion — cautious criticism, not celebration or dismissal.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same digitisation passage. Which statement is best supported?
o: All litigants now have equal access
Access gains from digitisation are uneven and depend on design choices
questions.e: The passage's thesis is that outcomes depend on whether design begins with the least connected user.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same digitisation passage. 'The great leveller in theory' implies technology is:
o: Expected to equalise access but may not in practice
questions.e: 'In theory' signals the expectation; the passage then shows practice can contradict it.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same digitisation passage. A suitable title would be:
o: The Digital Divide at the Courthouse Door
questions.e: The passage centres on how digitisation risks excluding the least connected litigants — the digital divide at courts.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: 'A society that silences dissent does not become more united; it becomes more brittle. The dissenter tests the strength of an argument the way stress tests a bridge — not to destroy it, but to reveal whether it can bear weight. Restrictions on speech are sometimes necessary, but every restriction should carry the burden of justification: the censor must show, not merely assert, that the harm is real, imminent, and unaddressable by narrower means.' The bridge analogy is used to argue that:
o: Dissent tests and thereby strengthens public reasoning
questions.e: Stress-testing reveals whether the bridge bears weight — dissent similarly tests arguments to reveal their strength.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same free-speech passage. According to the author, a restriction on speech is acceptable when:
o: The censor shows real, imminent harm unaddressable by narrower means
questions.e: The passage demands the censor show harm that is real, imminent and not addressable by narrower means.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same free-speech passage. 'Brittle' in context most nearly means:
questions.e: Contrasted with 'united', brittle means fragile — a silenced society breaks rather than bends.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same free-speech passage. The author's position is best described as:
o: Qualified defence of speech with a high bar for restrictions
questions.e: The author allows necessary restrictions but places a heavy burden of justification on the censor — a qualified defence.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same free-speech passage. Which claim would the author most likely reject?
o: Silencing critics makes a society resilient
Harm must be shown, not asserted
questions.e: The passage says silencing dissent makes society brittle, not resilient.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same free-speech passage. 'Carry the burden of justification' means the censor must:
questions.e: Bearing the burden of justification means demonstrating, with evidence, that the restriction is warranted.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: 'The promise of free legal aid rings hollow for the undertrial who has never heard of it. Statutes confer rights; awareness delivers them. Studies repeatedly show that the barrier is not the absence of law but the absence of knowledge — the prisoner who does not know a legal-aid clinic exists is, for all practical purposes, without counsel. Rights uncommunicated are rights unexercised.' The main argument is that:
o: Awareness is the decisive gap between legal aid on paper and in practice
Legal aid laws should be repealed
questions.e: The passage locates the failure in lack of knowledge, not lack of law: uncommunicated rights go unexercised.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same legal-aid passage. 'Rings hollow' most nearly means:
o: Sounds impressive but is empty in practice
questions.e: 'Rings hollow' is the idiom for something that sounds good but lacks substance.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same legal-aid passage. The author would most likely support:
questions.e: Since awareness is the gap, the author would back measures that communicate rights, like legal literacy in prisons.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same legal-aid passage. The tone is best described as:
questions.e: The passage is a serious critique of the awareness gap, earnest rather than mocking or detached.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same legal-aid passage. 'For all practical purposes' signals that:
o: The practical outcome equals having no counsel
questions.e: The phrase means that in effect, the unaware prisoner is in the same position as one without counsel.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same legal-aid passage. An assumption underlying the argument is:
o: Knowing about legal aid leads more prisoners to use it
questions.e: The argument that awareness is the barrier assumes that informed prisoners would actually seek and use the aid.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The committee's report was exhaustive, covering every district.' Exhaustive here means:
questions.e: Exhaustive means covering all aspects thoroughly; here it describes the report's comprehensiveness.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'Her argument was cogent and persuaded the bench.' Cogent means:
questions.e: Cogent describes reasoning that is clear, logical and convincing.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The witness gave an equivocal answer.' Equivocal means:
o: Open to more than one interpretation; ambiguous
questions.e: Equivocal means deliberately ambiguous, allowing multiple interpretations.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The judge's laconic reply ended the debate.' Laconic means:
questions.e: Laconic means using very few words — concise to the point of seeming terse.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'His profligate spending emptied the trust fund.' Profligate means:
questions.e: Profligate means recklessly extravagant and wasteful, especially with money.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The reform was lauded as sagacious.' Sagacious means:
questions.e: Sagacious means having or showing keen judgment; wise.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'A tenuous link connected the accused to the crime.' Tenuous means:
questions.e: Tenuous means thin, weak and having little substance.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The magistrate remained implacable despite the plea.' Implacable means:
questions.e: Implacable means not able to be calmed or appeased; relentlessly unyielding.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The new rule proved efficacious in reducing pendency.' Efficacious means:
o: Effective in producing the desired result
questions.e: Efficacious means successful in producing the intended outcome.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'His perfunctory inspection missed the defect.' Perfunctory means:
o: Carried out with minimal effort; superficial
questions.e: Perfunctory describes action done with little care or interest — merely going through the motions.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The counsel's perspicacious questions exposed the lie.' Perspicacious means:
questions.e: Perspicacious means having keen insight and discernment.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'An intransigent stance stalled the negotiations.' Intransigent means:
questions.e: Intransigent means refusing to change one's position; uncompromising.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The verdict vindicated the whistleblower.' Vindicated means:
questions.e: To vindicate is to clear of accusation or show to be right.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The data was spurious.' Spurious means:
questions.e: Spurious means not being what it purports to be; false or fake.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'She showed exemplary probity in office.' Probity means:
questions.e: Probity is the quality of having strong moral principles; honesty and integrity.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The law's ramifications were far-reaching.' Ramifications means:
questions.e: Ramifications are the complex consequences or implications of an action or decision.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'His testimony was corroborated by CCTV footage.' Corroborated means:
questions.e: To corroborate is to confirm or give support to a statement or theory.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The policy was rescinded after protests.' Rescinded means:
questions.e: Rescind means to revoke, cancel or repeal a law, order or agreement.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'A meticulous clerk keeps flawless records.' Meticulous means:
o: Showing great attention to detail; careful
questions.e: Meticulous means showing great care and precision about detail.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The speaker's rhetoric was inflammatory.' Inflammatory here means:
questions.e: Inflammatory rhetoric is language intended to provoke anger or unrest.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the correct sentence (neither/either agreement):
o: Neither of the lawyers were present
Neither of the lawyers have been present
Neither of the lawyers are present
Neither of the lawyers was present
questions.e: 'Neither' is singular; the verb must be 'was', not 'were'.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the correct sentence (collective noun agreement):
o: The committee has submitted their report
The committee have submitted their report
The committee has submitted its report
The committee have submitted its report
questions.e: A collective noun acting as one unit takes a singular verb and singular pronoun: 'has ... its'.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Identify the sentence with correct subject-verb agreement:
o: The list of cases have been long
The list of cases are long
The list of cases is long
The list of cases were long
questions.e: The subject is 'list' (singular); the intervening phrase 'of cases' does not change the verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence:
o: The judge who was impartial delivered the verdict.
The judge, who was impartial delivered the verdict
The judge, who was impartial, delivered the verdict
The judge who was impartial, delivered the verdict
questions.e: A non-restrictive clause ('who was impartial') is set off by commas on both sides.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Select the sentence with the correct use of the apostrophe:
questions.e: Singular possessive: 'witness's'; the verb 'was' must agree with singular 'testimony'.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the correct form: 'She is one of the advocates who ___ argued before the Constitution Bench.'
questions.e: The relative clause refers to 'advocates' (plural), so the verb is 'have argued'.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Fill in the blank: 'The court directed the parties to file replies ___ two weeks.'
questions.e: 'Within two weeks' sets a deadline; 'in two weeks' suggests the action occurs after two weeks pass.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the correct sentence (adjective + preposition):
