o: He is more senior than me in service
He is senior than me in service
He is senior from me in service
He is senior to me in service
questions.e: 'Senior' takes the preposition 'to', not 'than'.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the correct sentence (comprise usage):
o: The evidence was comprised of three documents
The evidence comprised of three documents
The evidence was comprised by three documents
questions.e: 'Comprise' means 'consist of'; the correct active form is 'comprised three documents', never 'comprised of'.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Identify the correctly worded sentence:
o: The reason of the delay was because the file was missing
The reason for the delay was that the file was missing
The reason for the delay is because the file was missing
The reason for the delay was because the file was missing
questions.e: 'The reason ... was that ...' is correct; 'the reason was because' is redundant.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the sentence with correct parallel structure:
o: The intern enjoys to read judgments, drafting notes, and arguing moots
The intern enjoys reading judgments, to draft notes, and arguing moots
The intern enjoys reading judgments, drafting notes, and to argue moots
The intern enjoys reading judgments, drafting notes, and arguing moots
questions.e: Parallel structure requires all gerunds: reading, drafting, arguing.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Select the correct reported speech: She said, 'I will file the appeal tomorrow.'
o: She says she would file the appeal the next day
She said she will file the appeal tomorrow
She said she would file the appeal tomorrow
She said she would file the appeal the next day
questions.e: In reported speech, 'will' becomes 'would' and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the correct active-voice conversion: 'The judgment was delivered by the bench.'
o: The bench had delivered the judgment
The bench has been delivering the judgment
questions.e: Past passive 'was delivered' converts to simple past active 'delivered'.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Fill in the blank with the correct article: '___ FIR was registered at midnight.'
questions.e: 'FIR' is pronounced 'eff-eye-aar', beginning with a vowel sound, so 'an' is correct.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the correct sentence (between/among):
o: Between the three judges, opinions differed
Between the judges, all three, opinions differed
Among the three judges, opinions differed
questions.e: 'Among' is used for more than two; 'between' is for two.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Identify the sentence with the misplaced modifier corrected:
o: Walking to the chamber, the clerk found the file
Walking to the chamber, the file was found
The file was found by the clerk walking to the chamber
The clerk found the file walking to the chamber
questions.e: The modifier 'walking to the chamber' must sit next to 'the clerk', the one walking.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the correct phrasal completion: 'The old precedent was ___ by the larger bench.'
questions.e: A larger bench 'overrules' an earlier precedent; 'overlooked' means failed to notice.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'To bite the dust' means:
questions.e: 'Bite the dust' is an idiom meaning to fail or be defeated.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'To burn the midnight oil' means:
o: To work late into the night
questions.e: The idiom means studying or working late at night.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'A blessing in disguise' refers to:
o: A seeming misfortune that turns out well
questions.e: A blessing in disguise is something that seems bad at first but results in good.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'To call a spade a spade' means:
questions.e: The idiom means to speak bluntly and call things by their right names.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The ball is in your court' means:
o: It is your turn to act or decide
questions.e: The idiom means the responsibility to act now lies with you.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Argument: 'The new metro line will reduce road congestion because commuters will switch to the metro.' The argument assumes that:
o: Commuters find the metro a preferable alternative and will actually switch
questions.e: The conclusion depends on commuters actually switching; if they do not find the metro preferable, congestion will not fall.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Argument: 'Online filing has made courts efficient, so pendency will now fall rapidly.' A necessary assumption is:
o: Filing delays were a significant cause of pendency
questions.e: Faster filing reduces pendency only if filing delays materially contributed to it.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Argument: 'Banning plastic bags will clean the city's drains.' The argument assumes:
o: Plastic bags form a significant part of drain blockages
questions.e: The ban cleans drains only if plastic bags are a significant cause of the blockage.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Argument: 'The coaching institute's toppers prove its teaching is the best.' The argument assumes:
o: Toppers joined because of the teaching
questions.e: Toppers prove teaching quality only if their success is attributable to the teaching rather than prior ability or other factors.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Statement: 'All successful litigants engaged senior counsel.' Conclusion: 'Engaging senior counsel guarantees success.' The flaw is:
o: Confusing a correlation/necessary condition with a sufficient one
questions.e: That all successful litigants had senior counsel does not make it sufficient for success; correlation is not sufficiency.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Argument: 'Crime rose after the new police chief took charge; therefore the chief caused the rise.' This reasoning is vulnerable because it:
questions.e: Post hoc reasoning mistakes sequence for causation; other factors may explain the rise.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: 'Most surveyed lawyers support the reform, so the Bar as a whole supports it.' The weakness is:
o: The sample may not represent the whole Bar
questions.e: Generalising from a survey requires a representative sample; a skewed sample invalidates the inference.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Argument: 'We should not listen to the economist's tax proposal because she once filed her returns late.' This commits the fallacy of:
questions.e: Attacking the proponent's character instead of the proposal's merits is an ad hominem fallacy.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: 'If we allow one exception to the rule, soon there will be no rule at all.' This is an example of:
questions.e: Predicting an inevitable slide from one step to disaster without showing the mechanism is a slippery-slope argument.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: 'Either we ban all vehicles or the city will choke; so ban all vehicles.' The flaw is:
o: False dilemma — intermediate options like regulation are ignored
questions.e: The argument presents only two extremes, ignoring middle paths such as phased regulation or public transport.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: 'The policy failed in two districts, so it will fail everywhere.' This is:
o: Hasty generalisation from a small sample
questions.e: Two districts are too small a base to generalise to all districts; the sample may be unrepresentative.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: 'The senior advocate says the interpretation is correct, so it must be.' This reasoning relies on:
o: Appeal to authority without independent reasons
questions.e: Deferring to an authority's say-so without examining reasons is the appeal-to-authority move.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: 'You oppose the dam; but you use electricity, so your objection is invalid.' This is:
o: Tu quoque — dismissing an argument because the arguer is allegedly inconsistent
questions.e: Pointing to the arguer's inconsistency does not refute the argument's merits; it is the tu quoque fallacy.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: 'The circular defines X; therefore X means what the circular says in all contexts.' The flaw is:
o: Equivocation — using a term in one context's sense across different contexts
questions.e: A term's meaning in one document cannot be imposed on every context; that shifts the term's sense (equivocation).

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: 'Nobody has proven the old bridge unsafe, so it is safe.' This commits:
questions.e: Treating absence of proof of danger as proof of safety is the appeal-to-ignorance fallacy.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: 'The last three Chief Justices favoured mediation, so the next one will too.' The reasoning is weak because:
o: Past preference does not determine a successor's independent view
questions.e: A successor's views are not fixed by predecessors'; the inference projects without a connecting reason.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Supporters of evening court sessions contend that holding trials after hours will cut the backlog of pending cases. Which finding most strengthens their case?
o: Pilot night courts in two districts disposed of 30% more cases per judge-month
questions.e: Evidence that night courts actually raised disposal rates directly supports the backlog-reduction claim.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: A proposal to run courts at night claims it would speed up disposal and clear long-pending matters. Which fact most weakens this proposal?
o: Most backlog cases require the same judges who already sit full day shifts, leaving no spare judicial capacity
questions.e: If the same judges must staff both shifts, no extra capacity is created, undermining the mechanism.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Some argue that raising the fee charged to file a suit will discourage people from bringing trivial or vexatious cases. Which evidence most supports this argument?
o: In a district that doubled fees, filings of low-value civil suits fell 40% while serious suits were unchanged
questions.e: A natural experiment showing frivolous-type filings fell while serious ones held steady directly supports deterrence.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Critics of a plan to hike litigation fees say it would not curb meritless suits. Which consideration most weakens the claim that higher fees deter frivolous litigation?
o: Frivolous litigants are typically wealthy parties for whom fees are trivial, while poor genuine litigants are priced out
questions.e: If fees bite the genuine poor rather than the frivolous rich, the policy misses its target — a direct weakener.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: It is claimed that installing cameras in courtrooms makes witnesses testify more truthfully. Which finding most strengthens this claim?
o: Studies show witnesses under observation give measurably more consistent testimony
questions.e: Empirical evidence linking observation to more consistent testimony supports the truthfulness mechanism.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Proponents say recording trials on video will improve the honesty of witness testimony. Which fact most undermines that assertion?
o: Witnesses reported feeling intimidated on camera and gave shorter, less complete answers
questions.e: If cameras intimidate witnesses into less complete answers, the claimed improvement reverses.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: A reform suggests compulsory mediation before any civil suit can be filed, expecting fewer cases to reach trial. Which fact most strengthens this proposal?
o: In jurisdictions with mandatory pre-suit mediation, nearly a third of disputes settled without trial
questions.e: Evidence of substantial settlement rates under mandatory mediation directly supports the pendency-cutting claim.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: It has been proposed that no civil suit be entertained until the parties attempt mediation, to reduce the load on courts. Which observation most weakens this proposal?
o: Where tried, unwilling parties used mediation only to delay, adding months before trial
questions.e: If mandatory mediation becomes a delaying tactic, it increases rather than reduces pendency.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Supporters of transparency argue that making judges' wealth declarations public will raise citizens' trust in the judiciary. Which finding most backs this view?
o: Surveys show trust rose in systems after asset disclosures became public
questions.e: Survey evidence of trust rising after disclosure directly supports the causal claim.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: A policy of publishing judges' asset declarations is defended on the ground that it will boost public confidence in courts. Which fact most weakens that defence?
o: In a pilot, published declarations were mined for sensational stories, and measured trust in courts fell
questions.e: Evidence that publication reduced trust directly contradicts the claim's predicted effect.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Advocates of televising parliamentary proceedings believe live coverage will make debates more policy-oriented and substantive. Which evidence most supports this belief?
o: Televised legislatures showed a measurable rise in policy-focused speeches
questions.e: Comparative evidence of more substantive speeches under telecast supports the claim.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: The proposal to allow cameras inside Parliament rests on the claim that broadcasts will improve the quality of debate. Which fact most undermines the claim?
o: Members played to the cameras with grandstanding, and substantive discussion time fell
questions.e: If cameras incentivise grandstanding over substance, the mechanism reverses.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: The makers of a new legal-aid app claim it will widen access to justice because it costs users nothing. Which fact most strengthens this claim?
o: Pilot users in remote blocks filed bail applications they had previously abandoned for lack of counsel
The app has a nice logo
questions.e: Evidence of previously excluded users actually obtaining relief through the app supports the access claim.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: An argument runs that a free legal-aid app will bring justice within reach of the poor. Which fact most weakens this argument?
o: Its interface is English-only, and most intended users in the pilot could not complete a single task
questions.e: If intended users cannot use the app, freeness is irrelevant and the access claim fails.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: It is claimed that strict attendance requirements for bar council members will improve discipline in the profession. Which finding most strengthens this claim?
o: Councils with enforced attendance showed fewer adjournments sought on counsel-absence grounds
questions.e: Fewer adjournments for absent counsel is direct evidence of improved discipline.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Advocates of tougher attendance rules say they will make the bar more disciplined. Which fact most weakens this assertion?
o: Enforcement drove junior lawyers out of practice without changing senior absenteeism
questions.e: If the rule harms juniors while missing the actual absentees, its disciplinary purpose is defeated.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: All contracts require consideration. No wagering agreement is enforceable as a contract. Which conclusion follows?
o: All unenforceable agreements are wagering agreements
No wagering agreement is a contract
questions.e: If no wagering agreement is enforceable as a contract, then none of them is a (valid) contract.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Some advocates are mediators. All mediators are trained neutrals. Which follows?
o: No advocate is a trained neutral
questions.e: The advocates who are mediators are within 'all mediators', hence trained neutrals — some advocates are trained neutrals.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: No fundamental right is absolute. Some restrictions are reasonable. Which follows?
o: No restriction can limit a right
Some restrictions may limit fundamental rights
questions.e: Non-absolute rights can be limited; reasonable restrictions are the mechanism — some restrictions may limit rights.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: All writs are constitutional remedies. Habeas corpus is a writ. Therefore:
o: Habeas corpus is the only writ
Habeas corpus is a constitutional remedy
questions.e: Classic Barbara syllogism: all W are R; H is W; therefore H is R.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Some judgments are unanimous. No unanimous judgment has a dissent. Which follows?
questions.e: The unanimous judgments (some judgments) are within the no-dissent class, so some judgments have no dissent.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: If a law is retrospective in criminal matters, it violates Article 20(1). This law is retrospective in a criminal matter. Therefore it:
questions.e: Modus ponens: the condition is satisfied, so the consequence follows.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Only registered deeds convey title to immovable property above the threshold value. This deed is unregistered. Therefore:
questions.e: 'Only if registered' makes registration necessary; its absence means no title passes.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: A will is valid only if attested by two witnesses. A will has three attesting witnesses. The will:
questions.e: 'Only if two' sets a minimum; three witnesses meet and exceed it.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Premises: 'Every valid notice was served in writing. This notice was served orally.' The valid conclusion is:
o: The notice was not a valid notice
questions.e: Contrapositive: valid → written; not written → not valid.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: 'All judges of the High Court are appointed by the President. X was appointed by the President.' Can we conclude X is a High Court judge?
o: No — affirming the consequent is invalid; others are also appointed by the President
questions.e: 'All A are B; X is B' does not yield 'X is A' — the converse is a fallacy.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Five witnesses A–E testify in order. B testifies immediately after A. D testifies before C but after B. E testifies last. Who testifies first?
questions.e: A is immediately followed by B; D after B but before C; E last. Order: A, B, D, C, E. First is A.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning
questions.q: Ravi sits between Sita and Gita. Sita is to the left of Ravi. Gita is to the right of Ravi. Who sits in the middle?
questions.e: 'Between' places Ravi in the middle, confirmed by the left/right statements.

questions.subject: Logical reasoning

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Fundamental Rights (Part III) are justiciable and enforceable by courts, while Directive Principles (Part IV) are non-justiciable guidelines for State policy. Courts have held the two supplementary, striving for harmonious construction rather than treating them as antagonistic. A law nationalising private buses to provide affordable rural transport is challenged as violating the right to carry on trade under Article 19(1)(g). The State defends it as implementing the Directive Principles on equitable distribution of resources. The court is most likely to:
o: Uphold the law without any scrutiny
Strike down the law because fundamental rights always override
Uphold the law if it imposes only a reasonable restriction in pursuit of a Directive Principle, reading the two harmoniously
questions.e: Courts read Parts III and IV harmoniously; a law advancing a Directive Principle can sustain a reasonable restriction on a fundamental right.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same FR/DPSP principle. A citizen files a writ petition demanding the court order the State to provide free housing to all, citing the Directive Principle on adequate livelihood. The petition is most likely to:
o: Succeed because Directive Principles are enforceable
Fail because the citizen is poor
Succeed because housing is a fundamental right explicitly
Fail because Directive Principles are non-justiciable and cannot be directly enforced by courts
questions.e: Directive Principles are expressly non-justiciable; courts cannot issue mandamus to enforce them directly.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same FR/DPSP principle. Parliament amends a fundamental right to better implement a Directive Principle. The amendment is challenged. The court will test it primarily against:
o: The basic structure doctrine, since even constitutional amendments cannot destroy essential features
questions.e: Since Kesavananda Bharati, amendments are valid only if they do not damage the basic structure, regardless of their DPSP purpose.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same FR/DPSP principle. A minimum-wages law restricts employers' freedom of trade but implements the Directive Principle of securing a living wage. The law is most likely:
o: Void because wages are private matters
Valid as a reasonable restriction advancing a Directive Principle
questions.e: Laws implementing Directive Principles, like living wages, are classic reasonable restrictions on trade freedoms.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same FR/DPSP principle. Which statement best captures the court's approach?
o: Fundamental rights and Directive Principles are complementary; courts harmonise them
Directive Principles are superior to fundamental rights
questions.e: The settled approach treats the two as supplementary — the Constitution's conscience and its enforceable core read together.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Criminal liability generally requires both a prohibited act (actus reus) and a blameworthy mental state (mens rea) such as intention, knowledge or recklessness, unless the statute creates strict liability. A hunter fires at what he genuinely and reasonably believes is a wild boar; it is a person, who dies. The hunter is most likely liable for:
o: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder, because the mental state for murder — intention or knowledge directed at a human — is absent on these facts
questions.e: Without intention or knowledge directed at causing a human's death, murder's mens rea is missing; liability falls to a lesser homicide category on a mistaken-belief fact pattern.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same mens rea principle. A shopkeeper sells a food item that unknowingly contains a banned additive; the statute expressly makes the seller liable 'irrespective of knowledge'. The shopkeeper is liable because:
o: He intended to sell banned goods
The statute creates strict liability, dispensing with mens rea
questions.e: Where the statute imposes liability irrespective of knowledge, it creates strict liability and mens rea need not be proved.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same mens rea principle. A person picks up another's identical umbrella from a stand, honestly believing it is his own. He is charged with theft. The best defence is:
o: Absence of dishonest intention — a bona fide mistake of fact negates the mens rea for theft
questions.e: Theft requires dishonest intention; an honest, reasonable mistake of fact negates the mental element.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same mens rea principle. A driver speeds through a crowded market at 100 km/h to thrill friends, killing a pedestrian. The mental state is best described as:
o: Recklessness/knowledge that death is likely, supporting culpable homicide
questions.e: Driving at lethal speed through a crowd shows knowledge that death is likely — the mens rea for culpable homicide.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same mens rea principle. Two persons plan a robbery; one waits outside as lookout while the other enters. Both are liable for the robbery because:
o: Common intention makes each liable for acts done in furtherance of the shared plan
questions.e: Common intention renders each participant liable for criminal acts done in furtherance of the shared design.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Natural justice requires (i) a fair hearing (audi alteram partem) and (ii) freedom from bias (nemo judex in causa sua). A university expels a student for misconduct without issuing any show-cause notice or hearing. The expulsion is most likely:
o: Valid if the misconduct was serious
Void only if the student is innocent
Void for violating audi alteram partem, since no hearing was given
questions.e: Expulsion without any notice or hearing denies the right to be heard, violating natural justice.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same natural justice principle. A licensing officer decides an appeal against his own original order rejecting a licence. The decision is vulnerable because:
o: Nemo judex in causa sua — no one should judge their own cause; the officer is biased in reviewing his own order
questions.e: Deciding an appeal against one's own order breaches the rule against bias.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same natural justice principle. Before cancelling a scholarship, the authority issues a show-cause notice, holds a hearing and gives a reasoned order. The procedure is:
o: Compliant only if the student agrees
questions.e: Notice, hearing and reasoned order satisfy both limbs of natural justice.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same natural justice principle. A selection committee member's daughter is a candidate, and he participates in her interview without disclosure. The selection is vulnerable because:
o: The member's personal interest creates a real likelihood of bias
questions.e: A personal interest in a candidate's success creates a real likelihood of bias, violating nemo judex in causa sua.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Same natural justice principle. In an urgent case where a building is about to collapse, the municipality demolishes it without prior hearing but holds a post-decisional hearing. This is most likely:
o: Justified because urgency may warrant a post-decisional hearing where prior hearing was impracticable
questions.e: Where immediate action is genuinely necessary, courts accept a prompt post-decisional hearing as substantial compliance.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: An agreement without consideration is void, except registered agreements out of natural love and affection between near relatives. A registered gift deed of a house by a father to his son is:
o: Valid only if stamped as a sale
Valid under the exception for registered agreements between near relatives
questions.e: Registered agreements made out of natural love and affection between near relatives are enforceable without consideration.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A contingent contract depends on an uncertain future event. A agrees to pay B ₹1,00,000 if B's ship returns safely. The ship sinks. A is:
o: Not liable because the contingency failed
questions.e: A contingent contract becomes enforceable only if the event happens; the sinking discharges the obligation.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: When a contract is broken, damages aim to place the injured party in the position performance would have. A supplier fails to deliver machinery; the buyer buys equivalent machinery at a higher price. Recoverable damages are:
o: The difference between the contract price and the reasonable substitute price, plus foreseeable losses
questions.e: The buyer is entitled to the additional cost of reasonable substitute performance and foreseeable consequential losses.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A minor's agreement is void; however, a guardian may contract for the minor's benefit. A guardian buys school books for a minor on credit. The seller can:
o: Not recover because minors cannot contract
Recover from the guardian, who contracted for the minor's benefit (necessaries)
questions.e: Contracts for a minor's necessaries/benefit through a guardian are enforceable against the guardian/minor's estate.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Novation substitutes a new contract for the old with all parties' consent, discharging the old. A owes B money; all three agree C will pay B instead of A. A's liability is:
questions.e: Novation with consent of all parties extinguishes the original obligation and substitutes the new one.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: In defamation, truth is a complete defence in civil law. A newspaper publishes true, documented facts about a contractor's blacklisting, causing him loss of business. The contractor's suit fails because:
o: Truth of the statement is a complete defence
questions.e: A true statement, however damaging, is not defamation; truth justifies the publication.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Fair comment on matters of public interest, honestly made, is protected. A critic writes that a publicly funded play was 'tedious and poorly directed'. The theatre company sues. The defence of fair comment:
o: Succeeds only with the director's consent
Succeeds if the comment is honest opinion on a matter of public interest based on true facts
Fails because the comment was negative
questions.e: Honest comment on a public performance, based on facts, is protected even if harsh.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: Contributory negligence reduces damages where the claimant's own fault contributed. A pedestrian crosses a highway at night in dark clothes away from the zebra crossing and is hit by a speeding driver. Damages will be:
o: Reduced to reflect the pedestrian's contributory negligence
questions.e: Both parties' fault contributed; damages are apportioned, reducing the award for the claimant's share of responsibility.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: An occupier owes lawful visitors a duty to keep premises reasonably safe. A mall leaves a polished floor wet without warning signs; a shopper slips. The mall is liable because:
o: Malls are strictly liable for everything
It breached its duty as occupier by leaving a known hazard unguarded and unwarned
questions.e: Occupiers must protect lawful visitors from known or foreseeable hazards; an unwarned wet polished floor breaches that duty.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A public nuisance is an unreasonable interference with a right common to the public. A factory discharges effluents into the village's only drinking-water stream. Affected villagers may sue because:
o: Drinking water is not a right
Only the State can sue for pollution
Pollution of a common water source is a public nuisance affecting the community's rights
questions.e: Fouling a community's sole drinking source unreasonably interferes with a public right, constituting public nuisance.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: 'Precedent is the law's memory. Without it, every dispute would begin from nothing and like cases would be decided unlike — the very definition of arbitrariness. Yet memory can become manacle: a rule forged for bullock carts should not govern bullet trains. The doctrine survives because it is not blind obedience; higher courts may overrule, and all courts may distinguish precedents whose reasons do not fit new facts.' The author's view of precedent is that it is:
o: Necessary but flexible — binding yet capable of being distinguished or overruled
questions.e: The passage defends precedent as necessary for consistency while stressing distinguishing and overruling keep it adaptable.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same precedent passage. 'Memory can become manacle' suggests precedent may:
o: Become a shackle when old rules are applied to new conditions
questions.e: A manacle is a shackle; the metaphor warns that rigidly following outdated rules constrains justice.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same precedent passage. 'Like cases decided unlike' is presented as:
questions.e: The text explicitly calls it 'the very definition of arbitrariness'.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same precedent passage. The bullock-cart/bullet-train contrast illustrates:
o: That rules made for old conditions may not fit new facts
questions.e: The contrast shows why distinguishing precedents is legitimate when facts and conditions change.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same precedent passage. The tone is best described as:
questions.e: The author weighs precedent's value against its risks — a balanced, reflective assessment.

questions.e: BNSS retains the 15-day police-custody ceiling of the CrPC scheme with procedural safeguards; label: statutory framework as enacted.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The 2024 Supreme Court ruling in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (EWS quota) — decided 2022, debated through 2024 — upheld the 103rd Amendment on the basis that:
o: Reservation solely on economic criteria does not violate the basic structure
Private institutions are exempt from all quotas
Economic criteria can never underlie reservation
questions.e: The 3:2 majority (Nov 2022) upheld EWS reservation, holding economic-criteria reservation does not breach the basic structure.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: In 2024, the Supreme Court held that a Speaker's delay in deciding disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule is:
o: Subject to judicial review, with courts able to set timelines
questions.e: The Court has repeatedly held that inordinate delay by Speakers in disqualification matters is subject to judicial review.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The 'One Nation One Election' proposal, advanced by a high-level committee in 2024, recommends:
o: Merging the ECI with State commissions
Simultaneous elections to Lok Sabha and State assemblies through constitutional amendments
questions.e: The Kovind committee (2024) recommended synchronised Lok Sabha and assembly elections via constitutional amendments and a common roll.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 establishes which enforcement body?
o: The Data Protection Board of India
questions.e: The DPDP Act creates the Data Protection Board of India to direct remedial measures and impose penalties.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: In 2025, amendments strengthening which aspect of arbitration law were most discussed in Indian legal commentary?
o: Institutional arbitration, timelines and limited court interference under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act framework
Making all awards final without challenge
questions.e: Commentary through 2024–25 centred on institutional arbitration, appointment reforms and curbing delays; label: trend, not a single enacted text.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Supreme Court's 2024 decision on LMV driving licences (Mukund Dewangan line of cases) clarified that:
o: A licence for light motor vehicles covers transport vehicles of that class without a separate endorsement
LMV licence holders need separate endorsements for transport vehicles
questions.e: The Constitution Bench (2024) held an LMV licence includes transport vehicles within the LMV class; no separate endorsement needed.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: In 2024, the Bombay High Court's Maratha reservation ruling context and the Supreme Court's stance reaffirmed that:
o: Reservation exceeding 50% requires exceptional circumstances with quantifiable data
questions.e: The Indra Sawhney 50% ceiling remains, breachable only in exceptional circumstances backed by quantifiable data.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Telecommunications Act, 2023 replaced:
o: The Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 and related colonial-era laws
questions.e: The Telecommunications Act, 2023 replaced the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 and the Indian Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: In 2023, the Supreme Court in Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India held regarding services in Delhi that:
o: Services belong to the municipal corporation
The Delhi government has legislative and executive power over services except public order, police and land
questions.e: The Constitution Bench held the elected Delhi government controls services, excluding the three reserved subjects — later altered by the 2023 GNCTD Amendment Act.

questions.subject: Legal current affairs
questions.q: The Press and Registration of Periodicals Act, 2023 replaced:
o: The Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867
questions.e: The PRP Act, 2023 replaced the colonial-era Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, simplifying title registration.

questions.subject: Quant
questions.q: A sum of ₹12,000 is divided between two parts such that simple interest on one part at 6% and on the other at 8% for 2 years is equal. The part at 6% is:

questions.subject: Quant
questions.q: A shopkeeper sells two items at ₹990 each, gaining 10% on one and losing 10% on the other. The net result is:
questions.e: CPs: 900 and 1100; total CP 2000, total SP 1980 → loss ₹20.

questions.subject: Quant
questions.q: If 15% of x equals 45, then x equals:

questions.subject: Quant
questions.q: The average of x, x+2, x+4, x+6 is 11. Then x equals:

questions.subject: Quant
questions.q: A train 150 m long running at 54 km/h crosses a man walking at 6 km/h in the same direction. Time taken is:
questions.e: Relative speed = 54 − 6 = 48 km/h = 13.33 m/s; time = 150/13.33 = 11.25 seconds.

questions.subject: Quant
questions.q: What percentage of 2 hours is 24 minutes?

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: 'A judgment is not a press release. Its audience is not the gallery but the losing party, who must be able to see — even in defeat — that reasons, not whim, decided the case. Prolixity buries reason; brevity without reasons is fiat. The discipline of judgment-writing is the discipline of showing one's work.' The central claim is that:
o: Judgments must display their reasoning so the loser sees the decision was reasoned, not arbitrary
questions.e: The passage's thesis: the losing party must see reasons, not whim — judgment-writing is showing one's work.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same judgment-writing passage. 'Prolixity buries reason' means:
questions.e: Prolixity is wordiness; burying reason means the reasoning gets lost in verbiage.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same judgment-writing passage. 'Brevity without reasons is fiat' implies:
o: A short order giving no reasons is mere command, not adjudication
questions.e: Fiat is an arbitrary decree; without reasons, brevity is just command, not reasoned adjudication.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Passage: Same judgment-writing passage. An assumption of the argument is:
o: A reasoned judgment increases acceptance of adverse outcomes
questions.e: The argument that reasons must be shown to the loser assumes shown reasons aid acceptance of defeat.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The advocate's argument was specious.' Specious means:
questions.e: Specious means misleadingly attractive; appearing true but actually false.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'An egregious error in the order led to its recall.' Egregious means:
questions.e: Egregious means remarkably bad, shocking in its badness.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'The committee reached a propitious moment to settle.' Propitious means:
questions.e: Propitious means indicating favourable conditions; opportune.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: 'His recalcitrant attitude frustrated the mediator.' Recalcitrant means:
o: Stubbornly resistant to authority or control
questions.e: Recalcitrant means obstinately uncooperative; resistant to direction.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the correct sentence (each + verb agreement):
o: Each of the petitions was dismissed
Each of the petitions are dismissed
Each of the petitions were dismissed
Each of the petitions have been dismissed
questions.e: 'Each' is singular; the verb must be 'was'.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Choose the correct sentence (data as mass noun):
o: The data show a clear trend
The data is showing a clear trend always
The datas show a clear trend
The data shows a clear trend
questions.e: In modern usage 'data' as a mass noun takes a singular verb: 'data shows'. (Strict Latin plural 'data show' is now rare.)

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A gift of immovable property must be registered to be valid. A orally gifts his house to his nephew and hands over possession. The nephew's title is:
o: Valid because it was oral and voluntary
Incomplete because registration is mandatory for gifts of immovable property
questions.e: Gifts of immovable property require a registered instrument; an oral gift passes no title.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A lease of immovable property for more than one year must be by registered instrument. A landlord orally grants a 5-year shop lease. The lease is:
o: Not valid as a 5-year lease for want of registration; at most a month-to-month tenancy may be implied
questions.e: A >1-year lease needs registration; an unregistered long lease cannot operate as such, though a monthly tenancy may be inferred.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Principle: A sale of immovable property worth ₹100 or more requires a registered deed. A pays ₹5,00,000 for a plot under an unregistered agreement. The buyer:
o: Does not get title without a registered conveyance
questions.e: Title to immovable property of that value passes only by registered instrument; payment and mutation alone do not convey title.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: The Transfer of Property Act primarily governs transfers:
o: Inter vivos (between living persons) of immovable property
questions.e: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 governs transfers of immovable property between living persons.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Under Section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act, which cannot be transferred?
o: A mere chance of an heir (spes successionis)
questions.e: Spes successionis — the chance of an heir apparent succeeding — is not transferable under Section 6(a).

questions.subject: Legal maxims
questions.q: 'Lis pendens' under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act means:
o: A pending suit; property under litigation cannot be dealt with so as to defeat the suit's outcome
questions.e: Lis pendens bars transfers of suit property that would affect the rights being litigated, binding purchasers to the decree.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The doctrine of basic structure holds that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 does not extend to destroying its essential features. The Supreme Court first articulated this limitation in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). Parliament later passed an amendment inserting a clause that declared "no amendment of this Constitution shall be called in question in any court on any ground." A citizen challenges an amendment that abolishes judicial review of constitutional amendments. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The amendment is valid because Article 368 places no limits on Parliament
The citizen's challenge fails because amendments are political questions
The amendment is valid since the basic structure doctrine applies only to fundamental rights
The ouster clause is struck down because judicial review is part of the basic structure
questions.e: Minerva Mills (1980) held that a limited amending power is itself part of the basic structure, and that clauses ousting judicial review of amendments destroy that structure; Parliament cannot use Article 368 to make its amending power unlimited.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 14 permits reasonable classification if it rests on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the law's object. The Supreme Court has also held that manifest arbitrariness in State action violates Article 14. A State rule grants mining leases only to applicants whose surnames begin with letters A–M, with no stated reason. An applicant named Zafar challenges the rule. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The rule is valid because the State may classify applicants in any manner it chooses
The challenge fails because Article 14 applies only to legislation, not executive rules
The rule survives because surnames are an intelligible differentia
The rule is struck down as manifestly arbitrary with no rational nexus to any legitimate object
questions.e: E.P. Royappa (1974) and Maneka Gandhi (1978) established that arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality; a classification with no rational connection to the law's purpose fails the twin test of Article 14.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression to citizens, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) on grounds including public order, decency and morality. A State bans a film solely because a pressure group threatens protests, although the censor board cleared it. The producer challenges the ban. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The ban is valid because preventing protests is a reasonable restriction
The producer has no remedy since films are not speech
The ban is valid because the State may impose prior restraint on any film
The ban fails because fear of protests by others is not a ground listed in Article 19(2)
questions.e: Article 19(2) permits restrictions only on the eight enumerated grounds; the State cannot suppress lawful expression merely because of a threatened heckler's veto, as the restriction must itself be reasonable and relatable to a listed ground.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 21 has been read to include the right to a speedy trial; inordinate delay in criminal proceedings can violate personal liberty. An undertrial has spent nine years in jail awaiting trial for an offence carrying a maximum sentence of seven years, with the delay caused by the prosecution seeking repeated adjournments. He seeks release. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: He is entitled to release because the delay itself violates Article 21
He must remain in jail until the trial concludes, whatever the delay
He can be released only if he proves his innocence first
Speedy trial applies only to civil cases, not criminal trials
questions.e: Hussainara Khatoon (1979) established that speedy trial is a fundamental right under Article 21, and prolonged pre-trial detention caused by systemic delay entitles the accused to release.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Under Article 32, any person may move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights, and the Court may issue writs including habeas corpus. Habeas corpus tests the legality of detention. A person detained under a preventive detention law is held for eight months without the grounds of detention being communicated to him. His family files a habeas corpus petition. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The petition fails because preventive detention is outside judicial review
The detention is set aside because Article 22(5) requires communication of grounds, and its breach makes continued detention illegal
The Court can only reduce the detention period, not quash it
Habeas corpus lies only against private detention, not State detention
questions.e: Article 22(5) mandates that the authority making a preventive detention order communicate the grounds to the detenu; failure to do so violates a constitutional safeguard and renders continued detention illegal, which habeas corpus corrects.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 15(1) prohibits the State from discriminating against citizens on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Article 15(3) permits special provisions for women and children. A State reserves 33% of seats in government medical colleges for women candidates. A male candidate challenges the reservation. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The reservation is struck down as discrimination on the ground of sex
The reservation is valid only if extended to private colleges too
The reservation is valid under Article 15(3), which expressly permits special provisions for women
Article 15(3) applies only to employment, not education
questions.e: Article 15(3) is an express exception to Article 15(1) allowing the State to make special provisions for women and children; such protective discrimination has been repeatedly upheld.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 16(1) guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment; Article 16(4) permits reservation for backward classes inadequately represented. In Indra Sawhney (1992), the Court capped reservations at 50% and excluded the creamy layer. A State provides 65% total reservation in government jobs. A general-category candidate challenges it. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The 65% reservation is valid because the 50% cap applies only to promotions
The cap does not apply because the State has special circumstances
The challenge fails because Article 16(4) is mandatory, not enabling
The excess over 50% is struck down as violating the equality mandate of Article 16
questions.e: Indra Sawhney laid down that total reservations under Articles 15(4) and 16(4) should not ordinarily exceed 50%, a ceiling the Court has treated as binding except in extraordinary situations with compelling justification.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The Preamble declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic. In SR Bommai (1994), the Supreme Court held secularism to be part of the basic structure. A State enacts a law declaring one religion the official religion of the State with preferential funding for its institutions. The law is challenged. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The law is valid because States may choose an official religion
The law is valid because secularism only binds the Union, not States
The challenge fails because the Preamble is not enforceable
The law is struck down because secularism, as part of the basic structure, forbids the State from identifying with or preferring any religion
questions.e: SR Bommai held secularism to be a basic feature of the Constitution, meaning the State must maintain principled distance from all religions and cannot establish or prefer one.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality and health. Courts apply the essential religious practices test from Shirur Mutt (1954). A religious group claims a recently invented ritual involving public obstruction is constitutionally protected. The State restricts it. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The restriction fails because courts cannot examine religious claims at all
The group wins because any sincerely held belief is automatically protected
Article 25 protects only individual belief, never group practices
The restriction is valid because only practices essential to the religion, as determined by the Court, receive Article 25 protection
questions.e: Under the essential religious practices doctrine, the Court determines which practices are truly essential to a religion; only those attract Article 25 protection, and even they remain subject to public order, morality and health.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 20(1) prohibits ex post facto criminal laws — no person shall be convicted for an act that was not an offence when committed, nor subjected to a greater penalty than what applied then. In 2024, a person committed an act punishable with two years' imprisonment. In 2025, Parliament raised the punishment for that offence to seven years. He is tried in 2026. Under the stated principle, the maximum sentence he can receive is:
o: Seven years, because the trial occurs after the amendment
Two years, because Article 20(1) bars retrospective enhancement of punishment
Seven years, because Article 20(1) applies only to the definition of offences
Two years, but only if he pleads guilty
questions.e: Article 20(1) embodies the rule against retrospective criminal punishment; an accused can only be subjected to the penalty prescribed at the time of commission of the offence.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 22 provides safeguards for arrested persons: production before a magistrate within 24 hours, the right to consult a legal practitioner, and information about grounds of arrest. D.K. Basu (1997) added enforceable arrest guidelines. Police arrest a person and hold him for four days without producing him before a magistrate or informing his family. He seeks compensation. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: He is entitled to compensation because the breach of Article 22 safeguards violates a fundamental right
No remedy exists because the police have discretion over production timelines
He can only seek departmental action against the officers
Article 22 applies only after a chargesheet is filed
questions.e: Nilabati Behera (1993) and D.K. Basu (1997) established that violation of Article 22 safeguards by State agents entitles the victim to monetary compensation through public law remedy under Articles 32 and 226.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 30(1) gives religious and linguistic minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. In TMA Pai (2002), the Court held the State may impose reasonable regulations in the interest of educational standards but cannot nationalise minority institutions. A State law takes over the management of all minority-run schools. The institutions challenge it. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The takeover is valid because the State may regulate minority institutions fully
The institutions must accept the takeover if compensated
The takeover is struck down because nationalisation destroys the Article 30(1) right to administer
Article 30(1) protects only the right to establish, not to administer
questions.e: TMA Pai held that while reasonable regulation for educational excellence is permitted, the State cannot destroy the core of the Article 30(1) right; taking over management amounts to nationalisation and is impermissible.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and "for any other purpose" — wider than Article 32, which is limited to fundamental rights. A person seeks a High Court writ against a State authority's order that violates a statutory right but no fundamental right. The authority objects that no fundamental right is involved. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The High Court cannot intervene because only the Supreme Court issues writs
The person must first exhaust all political remedies
Article 226 is available only against private parties
The High Court can intervene because Article 226 extends to any other purpose including legal rights
questions.e: Unlike Article 32, which is confined to fundamental rights, Article 226 expressly permits High Courts to issue writs for any other purpose, covering violations of legal and statutory rights by State authorities.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The doctrine of pith and substance resolves conflicts where a legislature appears to encroach on another's field: courts examine the true nature and character of the law. A State law imposing a tax on the sale of goods is challenged as trenching on the Union's powers, though its dominant purpose is raising State revenue from intra-state trade. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The law is void because any incidental encroachment invalidates it
The law is valid only with Presidential assent
The law is valid if its pith and substance falls within the State List, notwithstanding incidental encroachment
Pith and substance applies only to criminal laws
questions.e: The pith and substance doctrine holds that a law is valid if its true nature and character falls within the enacting legislature's competence, even if it incidentally touches another List's field.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 13(2) prohibits the State from making any law that takes away or abridges fundamental rights, and such laws are void to the extent of contravention. A post-Constitution State law bans all public meetings, violating Article 19(1)(b). The State argues the law serves public convenience. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The law stands because public convenience justifies it
The law is valid because Article 13 applies only to constitutional amendments
The citizens must seek amendment of the Constitution instead
The law is void to the extent it abridges Article 19(1)(b), since no Article 19(2)–(6) ground supports a total ban
questions.e: Under Article 13(2), any post-Constitution law inconsistent with fundamental rights is void to the extent of the inconsistency; a blanket ban on public meetings cannot be saved without a reasonable restriction relatable to Article 19(3).

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 21A makes free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 a fundamental right, implemented through the Right to Education Act, 2009. A State closes all government primary schools in rural districts, offering no alternative. Parents challenge the closure. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The closure violates Article 21A because the State has a constitutional duty to provide free elementary education
The State may close schools as a policy matter beyond judicial review
The parents must approach the legislature, not the courts
questions.e: Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) casts a direct constitutional obligation on the State to provide free and compulsory education to children between 6 and 14; dismantling the only available schooling breaches that duty.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The freedom of the press is implicit in Article 19(1)(a). In Bennett Coleman (1973), restrictions on newsprint that cripple newspapers were struck down. A government order caps newspaper pages to reduce criticism, claiming paper shortage though supplies are ample. Publishers challenge it. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The order is valid as a reasonable regulation of commerce
Publishers have no standing to challenge executive orders
The order is struck down as a direct and immediate infringement of press freedom under Article 19(1)(a)
Press freedom protects only government-owned media
questions.e: Bennett Coleman held that restrictions which directly and immediately curtail circulation of newspapers infringe Article 19(1)(a); a pretextual page cap aimed at stifling criticism is not a reasonable restriction.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Preventive detention is permitted by Article 22(3)–(7) but subject to strict safeguards, including review by an Advisory Board within three months. A person is preventively detained for six months without any reference to an Advisory Board. He challenges the detention. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The detention continues because preventive detention needs no review
The Advisory Board requirement applies only to convicted prisoners
The detention beyond three months without Advisory Board review is illegal under Article 22(4)
The detenu must wait for the full detention period to expire
questions.e: Article 22(4) mandates that preventive detention beyond three months requires the opinion of an Advisory Board; detention continued without such review violates the Constitution and must be set aside.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 31C, as interpreted in Minerva Mills (1980), protects only laws giving effect to Articles 39(b)–(c) from Articles 14 and 19 challenges. A State law nationalising private buses claims Article 31C protection though it implements no directive principle. The owners challenge it. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: Article 31C shields the law automatically once the State invokes it
The law cannot claim Article 31C protection because it does not genuinely give effect to Articles 39(b)–(c)
The owners have no remedy after nationalisation
questions.e: Minerva Mills confined Article 31C's protective umbrella to laws truly giving effect to the directive principles in Articles 39(b) and (c); a law must satisfy that nexus and cannot claim the shield by mere assertion.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 19(1)(d) guarantees freedom to move freely throughout India, subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public or protection of Scheduled Tribes. A State bars all citizens of other States from entering it without a permit, citing no specific threat. A traveller challenges the bar. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The bar is valid because States control their borders
The bar violates Article 19(1)(d) because a blanket entry ban is not a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public
The traveller needs Presidential permission first
Article 19(1)(d) applies only to international travel
questions.e: A total ban on inter-state movement bears no reasonable nexus to any Article 19(5) ground; such blanket restrictions on the freedom of movement have been struck down as disproportionate.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The right to privacy was declared a fundamental right under Article 21 in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017), subject to a three-fold test: legality, legitimate aim, and proportionality. A State mandates collection of citizens' fingerprints and iris scans for accessing all public parks, with no law authorising it. A citizen challenges the mandate. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The mandate is valid because privacy yields to administrative convenience
The mandate fails the Puttaswamy test at the first step because no law authorises the biometric collection
The citizen must prove actual misuse of data first
Privacy protects only against private actors
questions.e: Puttaswamy requires any State infringement of privacy to satisfy legality, legitimate aim and proportionality; a biometric mandate with no authorising law fails the legality requirement outright.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 15(5), inserted by the 93rd Amendment (2005), permits the State to make special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes in admissions to educational institutions, including private unaided ones except minority institutions. A State reserves seats for backward classes in private unaided non-minority colleges. The colleges challenge it. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The reservation is struck down because private colleges are beyond State regulation
Article 15(5) applies only to government colleges
The reservation is valid under Article 15(5) as upheld in Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008)
The colleges can defeat it by claiming minority status without proof
questions.e: Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008) upheld the 93rd Amendment and Article 15(5), permitting reservations in private unaided (non-minority) educational institutions for backward classes.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Under the basic structure doctrine, free and fair elections are an essential feature of the Constitution. A constitutional amendment abolishes all future elections to the Lok Sabha, replacing them with nomination by the ruling party. It is challenged. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The amendment is struck down because democracy and free elections form part of the basic structure
The amendment is valid because Article 368 is unlimited
The amendment is valid because elections are a statutory matter
Only the Election Commission can challenge such amendments
questions.e: Kesavananda Bharati and subsequent cases recognise democracy, including free and fair elections, as part of the basic structure; an amendment destroying representative democracy exceeds Parliament's amending power.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 20(3) protects an accused from being compelled to be a witness against himself. In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), involuntary narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests were held violative of Article 20(3) and Article 21. Police forcibly subject an accused to narco-analysis without consent and seek to use the revelations at trial. The accused objects. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The results are admissible because scientific tests are reliable
The involuntary test results are inadmissible because compelled self-incriminatory techniques violate Articles 20(3) and 21
The results are admissible if a magistrate approved the test
Article 20(3) applies only to oral testimony in court
questions.e: Selvi held that involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraph and BEAP tests amounts to compelled testimony violating Article 20(3) and the Article 21 right against cruel, inhuman treatment; only voluntary tests with safeguards are permissible.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 14's guarantee extends to non-citizens within Indian territory for most purposes. A State denies emergency medical treatment at a government hospital to a foreign national injured in an accident, citing his nationality. He challenges the denial. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The denial is valid because Article 14 protects only citizens
Foreign nationals have no constitutional rights in India
Hospitals may discriminate on any ground they choose
The denial violates Article 14 because the right to emergency medical care under Article 21 read with Article 14 extends to all persons
questions.e: Article 14 uses the word 'person', not 'citizen', and the Supreme Court has held the right to emergency medical treatment under Article 21 extends to everyone within the territory, regardless of nationality.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The doctrine of harmonious construction requires that apparently conflicting constitutional provisions be read together so that both survive. Articles 19(1)(a) (speech) and 19(1)(g) (profession) both seem engaged when a law regulates newspaper advertisements. A court must interpret the provisions. Under the stated principle, the correct approach is:
o: Strike down one of the two provisions as redundant
Apply only Article 19(1)(g) and ignore Article 19(1)(a)
Refer the conflict to Parliament for amendment
Read both provisions together, giving effect to each without destroying the other
questions.e: Harmonious construction mandates that provisions of the Constitution be interpreted so as to give effect to all of them; no provision is treated as redundant and none is allowed to defeat another.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 32(3) permits Parliament to empower other courts to issue writs, but the right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 is itself a fundamental right that cannot be suspended except during Emergency under Article 359. During a period when no Emergency is in force, Parliament passes a law barring citizens from approaching the Supreme Court for habeas corpus. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The bar is valid because Parliament controls court procedure
The bar is valid for habeas corpus but not other writs
The bar is unconstitutional because the Article 32 remedy is itself a fundamental right that cannot be abridged outside Emergency
Citizens may still approach High Courts, so no violation occurs
questions.e: Ambedkar called Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution; the guaranteed remedy is itself a fundamental right, and Parliament cannot suspend or abridge it except as provided in Article 359 during a proclaimed Emergency.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 19(6) permits reasonable restrictions on the freedom of profession in the interests of the general public, including professional qualifications. A State requires all practising architects to hold a recognised degree and register with the council, applying the rule prospectively. An unqualified practitioner challenges it. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The requirement is struck down because it restricts the freedom of profession
The requirement is valid as a reasonable restriction prescribing professional standards in the public interest
The State must compensate unqualified practitioners
questions.e: Prescribing minimum qualifications and registration for professions affecting public safety is a classic reasonable restriction under Article 19(6), repeatedly upheld as serving the general public interest.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Article 51A lists fundamental duties, including the duty to safeguard public property and abjure violence. Though duties are not directly enforceable, courts use them to interpret the reasonableness of restrictions. A law penalising wilful destruction of public buses during protests is challenged as violating free speech. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The law is struck down because duties are unenforceable
The law is upheld because preventing destruction of public property is a reasonable restriction and Article 51A supports reading the law to protect public property
The law is valid only if no penalty is prescribed
questions.e: Courts have held that fundamental duties, while not directly enforceable, guide the interpretation of reasonable restrictions; penalising violent destruction of public property is a permissible restriction on expression and assembly.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The Supreme Court's power of judicial review over legislative action flows from Articles 13, 32, 141, 142 and 144, and is part of the basic structure. A State legislature passes a resolution declaring that its laws "shall not be subject to review by any court." A citizen challenges a law passed under that resolution. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The declaration is ineffective because judicial review is part of the basic structure and cannot be ousted by legislation or resolution
Courts must respect the legislature's declaration and decline review
The citizen must seek the Governor's assent first
Judicial review applies only to Union laws
questions.e: Judicial review is a basic feature of the Constitution; no legislature can immunise its laws from constitutional scrutiny by a mere declaration, as Articles 13 and 32 entrench the courts' review power.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, which replaced the Indian Penal Code, the offence of murder is defined in Section 101 and culpable homicide in Section 100. A shoots B with the intention of causing death, and B dies. A claims he should be tried only for culpable homicide because the new code uses different terminology. Under the stated principle, the correct position is:
o: A is right because BNS abolished the distinction between murder and culpable homicide
A is liable for murder under Section 101 BNS because intention to cause death with a lethal act constitutes murder
A can be convicted only of attempt because BNS requires premeditation for murder
BNS applies only to offences committed before 1 July 2024
questions.e: BNS Sections 100 and 101 retain the IPC's culpable homicide/murder distinction; an act done with the intention of causing death that results in death is murder under Section 101, punishable with death or life imprisonment.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 69 of the BNS punishes sexual intercourse by deceitful means — including a promise to marry made without any intention of fulfilling it — where the act does not amount to rape; the punishment may extend to ten years' imprisonment plus fine. A genuine promise later broken for unavoidable reasons is not deceit. A promises to marry B with no intention of doing so from the start, and has sexual intercourse with her on that promise. She complains. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: A is liable for rape under BNS Sections 63–64 because the consent was vitiated
A is liable under BNS Section 69 for sexual intercourse by deceitful means, not rape
No offence is made out because B consented
A is liable only for cheating under BNS Section 318
questions.e: BNS 69 is the lex specialis for this exact pattern: a promise to marry made without any intention of fulfilment, where the intercourse does not amount to rape. It carries up to ten years' imprisonment and fine. Labelling it rape under Sections 63–64 is wrong because Section 69 expressly covers intercourse ‘not amounting to the offence of rape’; and a mere subsequent failure to marry, without initial deceitful intent, is neither rape nor a Section 69 offence.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 152 of the BNS punishes acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India, replacing the colonial sedition provision (Section 124A IPC). Unlike the old law, it targets secessionist and separatist activity. A journalist publishes a critical editorial about the government's economic policy without advocating secession or violence. She is charged under Section 152 BNS. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: She is liable because any criticism of the government endangers sovereignty
The charge fails because mere criticism of government policy, without incitement to secession or armed rebellion, does not attract Section 152
Section 152 applies to all published criticism
The charge succeeds because journalists enjoy no free speech protection
questions.e: Section 152 BNS, like the Kedar Nath (1962) reading of sedition, requires acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity — incitement to secession, armed rebellion or separatist activity; bona fide criticism of government policy is protected speech.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure. Section 173 BNSS governs information relating to cognizable offences (FIRs) and expressly permits registration of a Zero FIR at any police station irrespective of territorial jurisdiction. A woman is robbed on a train; she reports it at a station in a different state. The officer refuses, saying the offence occurred outside his jurisdiction. Under the stated principle, the officer's refusal is:
o: Valid, because FIRs can only be registered where the offence occurred
Invalid, because Section 173 BNSS permits Zero FIR registration at any police station regardless of jurisdiction
Valid, because railway offences are excluded from BNSS
Invalid only if the victim is a woman
questions.e: BNSS Section 173 institutionalises Zero FIR: information about a cognizable offence may be recorded at any police station irrespective of where the offence was committed, and then transferred to the jurisdictional station.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 35 of the BNSS (corresponding to Section 41A CrPC) provides that where arrest is not required under the criteria stated in the section, the police shall issue a notice of appearance; where arrest is made in an offence punishable with seven years or less, the reasons must be recorded. In Arnesh Kumar (2014), the Supreme Court made compliance with these safeguards mandatory and required magistrates to verify it. Police arrest a first-time accused in a cheating case punishable with five years' imprisonment without issuing any notice and without recording reasons. Under the stated principle, the arrest is:
o: Illegal because Section 35 BNSS and Arnesh Kumar require a notice of appearance where arrest is not required, and recorded reasons where arrest is made — neither was done here
Valid because police have absolute discretion to arrest
Valid because cheating is a serious economic offence
Illegal only if the accused is a woman
questions.e: Arnesh Kumar (2014), now reflected in BNSS Section 35, makes the safeguards mandatory: notice of appearance where arrest is not required under the statutory criteria, and recorded reasons where arrest is made in offences carrying seven years or less. An arrest that does neither is illegal, and magistrates must verify compliance.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023, Section 23(1) provides that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved against the accused. Section 26 permits a dying declaration to be relevant. A, in police custody, confesses to a constable that he committed a theft, and separately tells a magistrate the same facts. At trial, the prosecution seeks to prove both statements. Under the stated principle:
o: Both are inadmissible because all confessions are barred
The confession to the constable is inadmissible under Section 23(1) BSA, but a confession before a magistrate, if voluntary, is admissible
The confession to the constable is admissible if corroborated
questions.e: BSA Section 23(1) (like Section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act) bars proof of confessions made to police officers against the accused, while judicial confessions recorded by a magistrate under proper safeguards remain admissible.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 85 of the BNS punishes cruelty by a husband or his relatives against a woman, corresponding to Section 498A IPC.
