In 2026, the Supreme Court in Dr. Lokesh B.H. held that a man in a relationship in the nature of marriage may face prosecution for cruelty under these provisions even without a legally valid marriage. A woman in a long-term live-in relationship alleges sustained cruelty by her partner. He claims Section 85 BNS cannot apply without marriage. Under the stated principle:
o: He can be prosecuted because the Court extended cruelty provisions to relationships in the nature of marriage
He is right because cruelty provisions require a valid marriage
Cruelty provisions apply only to dowry demands
Live-in relationships are illegal, so no prosecution is possible
questions.e: In Dr. Lokesh B.H. v. State of Karnataka (2026), the Supreme Court held that a relationship in the nature of marriage can attract prosecution for cruelty under Section 498A IPC/Section 85 BNS, though the interpretation is confined to those cruelty provisions.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 103(2) of the BNS creates the offence of murder by a group of five or more persons acting in concert on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language or personal belief — commonly called mob lynching. A mob of eight persons kills a man because of his community identity. They claim it is only ordinary murder. Under the stated principle:
o: They are liable under Section 103(2) BNS, which prescribes death or life imprisonment for murder by a mob acting on identity-based grounds
They are right because BNS has no separate mob-lynching provision
Section 103(2) applies only to groups smaller than five
Mob lynching is punishable only with a fine
questions.e: BNS Section 103(2) specifically criminalises murder committed by five or more persons acting in concert on identity-based grounds including community, with punishment of death or life imprisonment and fine.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 304 of the BNS creates the distinct offence of snatching — sudden, quick seizure of movable property from a person. A snatches a woman's handbag and flees on a motorcycle. He argues it is only ordinary theft under Section 303. Under the stated principle:
o: He is right because snatching is just a form of theft
He is liable for snatching under Section 304 BNS, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment
Snatching requires the use of weapons
Section 304 applies only to chain-snatching of gold
questions.e: BNS introduced snatching as a standalone offence in Section 304, distinct from theft under Section 303, recognising the sudden-force element; it carries imprisonment up to three years.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 111 of the BNS defines organised crime and Section 113 defines terrorist acts, both new dedicated provisions. A syndicate runs an inter-state racket of kidnapping for ransom with a structured hierarchy. Members claim they can only be tried for individual kidnappings. Under the stated principle:
o: They can be prosecuted for organised crime under Section 111 BNS, which targets continuing unlawful activity by an organised crime syndicate
They are right because organised crime is not defined in Indian law
Section 111 applies only to economic offences
Organised crime charges require prior sanction of the President
questions.e: BNS Section 111 defines and punishes organised crime — continuing unlawful activity by an organised crime syndicate — with severe penalties including death in cases resulting in death, going beyond individual substantive offences.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Under BNSS Section 187 (corresponding to Section 167 CrPC), a magistrate may authorise detention of an accused for a total of 90 days where the investigation relates to offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or ten years or more, and 60 days otherwise; default bail follows. An accused in a murder case has been in custody for 95 days without a chargesheet. He seeks default bail. Under the stated principle:
o: He is entitled to default bail because the 90-day period for offences punishable with death or life imprisonment has expired without a chargesheet
He is not entitled to bail because murder is a heinous offence
Default bail applies only to bailable offences
The magistrate may extend custody indefinitely in murder cases
questions.e: BNSS Section 187 preserves the CrPC Section 167 scheme: if investigation is not completed within 90 days for grave offences (60 for others), the accused acquires an indefeasible right to default bail.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 63 of the BSA (corresponding to Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act) governs admissibility of electronic records and requires a certificate for secondary electronic evidence. The prosecution seeks to rely on CCTV footage copied onto a pen drive without producing any certificate. The defence objects. Under the stated principle:
o: The footage is admissible without a certificate because it is primary evidence
Certificates are required only for emails, not video
The objection succeeds because Section 63 BSA mandates a certificate for admissibility of electronic records produced as secondary evidence
The court may admit it at its discretion without conditions
questions.e: Anvar P.V. (2014) and Arjun Panditrao (2020), now reflected in BSA Section 63, require a certificate as a condition precedent for admissibility of electronic records produced as secondary evidence.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 26 of the BSA (corresponding to Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act) makes a dying declaration relevant when it relates to the cause of death. A victim, fully conscious and certified fit by a doctor, names her attacker before dying. The defence argues it is inadmissible hearsay. Under the stated principle:
o: The defence is right because the victim cannot be cross-examined
Dying declarations require corroboration in every case
Dying declarations are admissible only in civil cases
The dying declaration is admissible under Section 26 BSA and can sustain conviction if found truthful and voluntary
questions.e: Section 26 BSA makes statements by a person as to the cause of their death relevant; a truthful, voluntary dying declaration recorded with a fitness certificate can be the sole basis of conviction.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 118 of the BSA (corresponding to Section 113B of the Indian Evidence Act) raises a presumption as to dowry death: where a woman dies by burns or bodily injury within seven years of marriage and cruelty for dowry is shown, the court shall presume the husband or relative caused the dowry death. A woman dies of burns within three years of marriage after documented dowry harassment. The husband claims the prosecution must prove he killed her. Under the stated principle:
o: The husband is right because the burden of proof never shifts
The court shall presume dowry death under Section 118 BSA once cruelty for dowry soon before death is proved, shifting the burden to the accused
The presumption applies only after ten years of marriage
Dowry death requires an eyewitness in all cases
questions.e: BSA Section 118 creates a mandatory presumption of dowry death where a woman dies unnaturally within seven years of marriage and was subjected to cruelty for dowry soon before death; the accused must then rebut it.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: BNS Section 80 punishes dowry death with imprisonment of not less than seven years, extendable to life. BNS Section 86 defines cruelty. A woman commits suicide within five years of marriage, and evidence shows persistent dowry demands and cruelty. The husband argues suicide cannot be dowry death. Under the stated principle:
o: He is right because dowry death requires homicide
Dowry death applies only to deaths by burning
The seven-year period runs from the complaint, not the marriage
Abetment of suicide through dowry-related cruelty can attract dowry death provisions where the statutory ingredients are met
questions.e: Dowry death under BNS Section 80 covers deaths caused by burns, bodily injury, or occurring otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of marriage where cruelty for dowry is shown; abetted suicides linked to dowry cruelty fall within its sweep.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 356 of the BNSS permits inquiry, trial and judgment in the absence of a proclaimed offender, but only with safeguards: the offender must have absconded to evade trial with no immediate prospect of arrest; the court must record reasons in writing; trial cannot commence until 90 days have lapsed from the framing of charge; two consecutive arrest warrants at least 30 days apart must have issued; notice must be published in a newspaper, given to a relative or friend, affixed at his residence and displayed at the police station; and an unrepresented offender gets State-funded counsel. An accused in an economic offence absconds after charges are framed and is declared a proclaimed offender, but the court starts his trial in absentia only 20 days after framing of charge, without issuing fresh warrants or recording reasons. He claims the trial is void. Under the stated principle:
o: He is wrong because proclamation alone validates trial in absentia
The trial is void because the 90-day post-charge wait, the warrant and notice procedure, and the written reasons required by Section 356 were not complied with
Section 356 applies only to petty offences
The court must wait indefinitely for the absconder
questions.e: Section 356(1)–(3) BNSS makes trial in absentia conditional, not automatic: no immediate prospect of arrest, reasons recorded in writing, 90 days from framing of charge, two warrants at least 30 days apart, newspaper/relative/affixation notices, and State-funded counsel for the unrepresented. Skipping these safeguards renders the in-absentia trial invalid.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 109 of the BNS specifically punishes attempt to murder: whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge that, had death resulted, he would be guilty of murder, is punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment and fine — and life imprisonment if hurt is caused (Section 62 is only the general attempt provision, applying where no express provision exists). A fires a gun at B intending to kill, but misses. A claims no offence is complete since B is unharmed. Under the stated principle:
o: A is right because attempt requires injury
Attempt applies only if the weapon is recovered
A is liable for attempt to murder under Section 109 BNS because firing the gun goes beyond mere preparation
A can be punished only for possessing the gun
questions.e: Attempt to murder has its own provision — BNS 109 (the old IPC 307) — punishing the act done with murderous intent even where death does not ensue; the general attempt provision (BNS 62) applies only where no express provision exists. Firing a gun at the victim goes beyond preparation and needs no resulting injury.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 61 of the BNS defines criminal conspiracy as an agreement between two or more persons to do an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means. A and B agree to forge property documents; B is arrested before any forgery occurs. A claims no conspiracy exists since nothing was forged. Under the stated principle:
o: A is right because conspiracy requires completion of the offence
Conspiracy requires at least three persons
A conspiracy is complete on the agreement itself; B's arrest does not erase the offence under Section 61 BNS
questions.e: Criminal conspiracy is complete the moment two or more persons agree to commit an illegal act; it is an inchoate offence and does not require the agreed offence to be attempted or completed.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 39 of the BSA (corresponding to Section 45 of the Indian Evidence Act) makes the opinions of experts in foreign science, art, handwriting or finger impressions relevant. In a forgery trial, the prosecution relies on a handwriting expert's opinion. The defence argues only eyewitnesses can prove forgery. Under the stated principle:
o: The defence is right because expert opinion is hearsay
Expert opinion is binding on the court
Handwriting experts are not recognised in Indian law
The expert's opinion is relevant under Section 39 BSA, though the court must independently evaluate it and it is not conclusive
questions.e: BSA Section 39 makes expert opinion relevant on points of foreign science or art including handwriting; however, expert evidence is advisory, and the court as the ultimate judge must assess it independently.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 104 of the BSA (corresponding to Section 101 of the Indian Evidence Act) places the burden of proving the existence of facts on whoever asserts them. In a murder trial, the prosecution must prove the accused caused the death. The accused claims the prosecution must also disprove his alibi. Under the stated principle:
o: The prosecution bears the burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt; the accused need only raise reasonable doubt, and must prove facts specially within his knowledge
The accused is right because the prosecution must disprove every defence
The accused must prove his innocence
questions.e: The prosecution must prove the offence beyond reasonable doubt under BSA Section 104; the accused bears no burden to prove innocence, though facts specially within his knowledge (Section 109 BSA) must be proved by him.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: BNS Section 318 punishes cheating in graded forms: simple cheating (Section 318(2)) carries up to three years, but cheating that dishonestly induces delivery of property (Section 318(4)) is punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment and fine. A sells a car concealing that it was in a major accident, inducing B to pay full price. A claims it is only a civil dispute. Under the stated principle:
o: A is right because all sale disputes are civil
A is liable for cheating under Section 318(4) BNS because dishonest concealment inducing delivery of property attracts up to seven years' imprisonment and fine
questions.e: Cheating by dishonest concealment inducing delivery of property falls under the aggravated form in BNS Section 318(4) (the old IPC 420), punishable with up to seven years plus fine — not the three-year simple-cheating clause; the criminal offence coexists with any civil remedy.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: BNS Section 356 punishes defamation with up to two years' imprisonment, retaining the ten exceptions from Section 499 IPC, including truth for public good. A journalist publishes a true report of a public official's corruption, made in good faith for the public good. The official files a defamation complaint. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: The journalist is liable because reputation is absolute
The publication is protected by the truth-for-public-good exception to defamation
Truth is never a defence to defamation in India
questions.e: The First Exception to defamation (BNS Section 356(1), carried over from IPC Section 499) protects imputations that are true and made for the public good; bona fide investigative reporting on a public official's corruption falls squarely within it.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 351 of the BNS punishes criminal intimidation: threatening injury to person, property or reputation to cause alarm. A threatens to burn down B's shop unless B withdraws a court case. A claims it was mere angry words. Under the stated principle:
o: A is liable for criminal intimidation under Section 351 BNS because the threat was made to compel B to drop legal proceedings
A is right because words alone cannot be intimidation
Threats relating to court cases are privileged
questions.e: Criminal intimidation under BNS Section 351 is complete when a threat of injury is made with intent to cause alarm or to compel someone to do or omit an act they are legally entitled to do, such as pursuing litigation.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Under BNSS, Section 283 provides for summary trials: Section 283(2) extends them to offences not punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment exceeding three years (after hearing the accused and recording reasons), while Section 285(2) caps the sentence in any summary trial at three months' imprisonment. A magistrate tries a theft case (punishable with up to two years) summarily and sentences the accused to two months' imprisonment. The accused claims summary trials are unconstitutional. Under the stated principle:
o: He is right because all criminal trials require full procedure
Summary trials are valid only with the accused's written consent
The magistrate exceeded his powers because summary trials cap sentences at one year
Summary trials under Sections 283–285 BNSS are constitutionally valid for specified minor offences, and the two-month sentence is within the Section 285 cap
questions.e: Summary procedure for minor offences is a constitutionally recognised proportionate process; BNSS Section 283 permits summary trial of offences punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, and Section 285(2) caps any summary-trial sentence at three months — the two-month sentence complies.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: BNS Section 115 punishes voluntarily causing hurt (up to one year), Section 116 defines grievous hurt, and Section 117 punishes voluntarily causing grievous hurt (up to seven years). Grievous hurt includes emasculation, permanent privation of sight or hearing, and fractures. A fractures B's arm in a fight. A claims it is only simple hurt. Under the stated principle:
o: A is right because fractures are simple hurt
The distinction between hurt and grievous hurt was abolished in BNS
A is liable for voluntarily causing grievous hurt under Section 117 BNS because fracture of a bone falls within the Section 116 definition of grievous hurt
questions.e: BNS retains the IPC's exhaustive list of grievous hurt, which expressly includes fracture or dislocation of a bone; such injury attracts Section 117 rather than Section 115.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 137 of the BNS punishes kidnapping (taking a minor or person of unsound mind from lawful guardianship), and Section 138 punishes abduction (compelling by force or deceitful means). A deceitfully lures an adult businessman into a car and confines him for ransom. A claims it is kidnapping. Under the stated principle, the correct classification is:
o: Abduction under Section 138 BNS, because the victim is an adult compelled by deceitful means
Neither, because ransom makes it extortion only
questions.e: Kidnapping under BNS Section 137 is confined to minors and persons of unsound mind taken from lawful guardianship; compelling an adult by force or deceit is abduction under Section 138.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The BNS introduces community service as a punishment for certain minor offences. The proviso to Section 303(2) provides that in theft cases where the value of the stolen property is less than ₹5,000 and the person is convicted for the first time, he shall, upon return of the value of the property or restoration of the stolen property, be punished with community service. A first-time offender steals goods worth ₹3,000 and restores them; the magistrate orders community service. The offender claims only imprisonment or fine are valid punishments. Under the stated principle:
o: The offender is right because community service is not recognised in Indian criminal law
Community service requires the victim's consent
Community service applies only to juvenile offenders
The order is valid because the proviso to Section 303(2) BNS prescribes community service where low value, first conviction and return or restoration of the property concur
questions.e: The BNS for the first time introduces community service as a statutory punishment; the Section 303(2) proviso makes it the prescribed punishment for petty first-time theft below ₹5,000 once the property's value is returned or the property restored.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Under BNSS Section 173, information about a cognizable offence may be given orally or in writing, including through electronic communication, and must be signed by the informant within three days if given electronically. A sends an email reporting a cognizable offence but never signs it. Police refuse to register the FIR. Under the stated principle:
o: The refusal is invalid because emails need no signature
The refusal is valid because BNSS requires the informant to sign electronic information within three days
FIRs can only be given orally
questions.e: BNSS Section 173 permits e-FIRs but requires the informant to sign the information within three days of giving it electronically; until signed, the information may be treated as incomplete.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: BNS Section 70 punishes gang rape with rigorous imprisonment of not less than twenty years, extendable to life. In a case of gang rape of an adult woman, the accused argue for leniency citing their youth. Under the stated principle, the court's sentencing discretion is:
o: Unlimited, because youth is always mitigating
Unlimited because minimum sentences are advisory
Constrained by the statutory minimum of twenty years' rigorous imprisonment under Section 70 BNS
The court may impose only a fine for first offenders
questions.e: BNS Section 70 prescribes a mandatory minimum sentence of twenty years' rigorous imprisonment for gang rape; courts cannot go below the statutory minimum regardless of mitigating circumstances.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 6 of the BSA (corresponding to Section 8 of the Indian Evidence Act) makes motive, preparation and conduct relevant as facts showing the state of mind. In a murder trial, the prosecution proves the accused bought poison days before the victim's poisoning. The defence calls it irrelevant. Under the stated principle:
o: The defence is right because only the killing act matters
Motive must be proved in every murder case
Preparation is relevant under Section 6 BSA as conduct showing intention and design
Preparation is relevant only in conspiracy cases
questions.e: BSA Section 6 expressly makes facts showing motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct relevant; preparation is admissible to establish design, though motive itself need not be proved in every case.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 requires free consent, capacity, lawful consideration and object, and no express voidness for a valid contract. Section 11 requires parties to be majors of sound mind. In Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903), the Privy Council held a minor's agreement void ab initio. A, aged 16, buys a laptop on credit from B, signing a promissory note. B sues on the note. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: B wins because A received the benefit of the laptop
B wins because necessaries are always recoverable
The note is valid because A signed it voluntarily
B's claim fails because a minor's agreement is void from the beginning and cannot be enforced
questions.e: Mohori Bibee established that a minor lacks contractual capacity under Section 11, so the agreement is void ab initio; it cannot be ratified on majority nor enforced, though necessaries supplied may be claimed against the minor's estate under Section 68.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 4 of the Indian Contract Act provides that communication of acceptance is complete against the proposer when it is put in a course of transmission, and against the acceptor when it comes to the proposer's knowledge. In Bhagwandas v. Girdharilal (1966), the Supreme Court held that for instantaneous communication like telephone, acceptance is complete when heard. A accepts B's offer by telephone, but the line disconnects before B hears the acceptance. Under the stated principle:
o: The contract is complete because A spoke the acceptance
The postal rule applies to telephones
A contract arises only after written confirmation
No contract is concluded because, for telephone acceptances, communication is complete only when heard by the proposer
questions.e: Bhagwandas (1966) distinguished instantaneous from non-instantaneous communication: for telephone acceptances, Section 4 requires the acceptance to come to the proposer's knowledge, so an unheard acceptance concludes no contract.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 25 of the Indian Contract Act declares agreements without consideration void, with exceptions including a promise in registered writing made on account of natural love and affection. A, out of natural love and affection, promises in a registered deed to pay his brother ₹5,00,000. He later refuses. Under the stated principle:
o: The promise is unenforceable for want of consideration
Registration cannot cure absence of consideration
The promise is enforceable because it falls within the first exception to Section 25 — registered writing motivated by natural love and affection
The exception applies only to immovable property
questions.e: Section 25(1) expressly saves agreements made in registered writing on account of natural love and affection between near relations; such promises are enforceable without consideration.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 27 voids agreements in restraint of trade, with a sole exception for the sale of goodwill where the seller agrees not to carry on a similar business within reasonable local limits. A sells his bakery's goodwill to B and agrees not to open a competing bakery within the same city for three years. A opens one after a year. Under the stated principle:
o: The restraint is valid under the goodwill exception to Section 27, and B can restrain A
The restraint is void because all restraints of trade are void
The restraint is valid only if A received no payment
Section 27 does not apply to bakeries
questions.e: The exception to Section 27 permits reasonable restraints ancillary to the sale of goodwill; a time- and area-limited non-compete given on sale of goodwill is enforceable.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 56 deals with initial and supervening impossibility; the doctrine of frustration discharges the contract when performance becomes impossible. In Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram (1954), wartime requisition frustrated a land-development contract. A contracts to let his specific concert hall to B for a music festival on a fixed date; before the date, the hall is destroyed by an earthquake through no fault of either party. Under the stated principle:
o: A must rebuild the hall or pay full damages
A must provide an alternative hall at any cost
Frustration applies only to government contracts
The contract is discharged by frustration under Section 56 because the specific subject matter, whose continued existence was the contract's foundation, was destroyed without fault
questions.e: On the Taylor v. Caldwell principle adopted in Satyabrata Ghose, Section 56 discharges a contract where supervening destruction of the specific subject matter — the foundation of the contract — makes performance impossible without either party's fault.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 73 provides compensation for loss naturally arising or within the parties' contemplation; Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) limits recovery to foreseeable losses. A mill owner tells a carrier the mill is stopped and delay will cost profits; the carrier delays delivery of a broken shaft. Under the stated principle on damages:
o: Only the carriage charges are recoverable
Lost profits are never recoverable in contract
Lost profits are recoverable because the special circumstances were communicated, bringing them within the parties' contemplation under the second rule in Hadley v. Baxendale
questions.e: Hadley v. Baxendale's second rule, embodied in Section 73, allows recovery of losses arising from special circumstances where those circumstances were communicated so that the loss was within the parties' contemplation.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 74 deals with stipulated sums: the aggrieved party is entitled to reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount named, and penalty clauses are not enforced as such. In Fate Chand v. Balkishan Dass (1964), the Court held only reasonable compensation is recoverable. A contract names ₹10,00,000 as damages for breach; actual loss is ₹1,00,000. Under the stated principle:
o: The full ₹10,00,000 is recoverable as agreed
No damages are recoverable when a sum is named
The court must award the named sum regardless of loss
Only reasonable compensation up to the named sum — here ₹1,00,000 — is recoverable, since Section 74 bars enforcement of penalties
questions.e: Fate Chand (1964), affirmed in Kailash Nath Associates (2015), holds Section 74 entitles the claimant only to reasonable compensation not exceeding the stipulated sum; extravagant penalty stipulations are cut down to actual reasonable loss.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 2(d) defines consideration as an act, abstinence or promise at the desire of the promisor. Past voluntary services rendered at the promisor's desire can support a later promise. A requests B to nurse his sick father; B does so for a month; A later promises to pay B ₹50,000 for the service. Under the stated principle:
o: The promise is void because the service was already rendered
The promise is enforceable because past services rendered at the promisor's desire constitute valid consideration
Past consideration is never valid in Indian law
The promise needs registration to be valid
questions.e: Indian law, unlike English law, recognises past consideration: Section 2(d) expressly includes acts done at the desire of the promisor, so services rendered at A's request support his subsequent promise.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: A general offer to the world at large, like the one in Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893), can be accepted by anyone who performs its conditions with knowledge of the offer. In Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt (1913), acceptance without knowledge of the offer was held ineffective. A company advertises a reward for returning a lost dog; B, unaware of the advertisement, returns the dog and then learns of the reward. Under the stated principle:
o: B can claim the reward because he returned the dog
B can claim half the reward
B cannot claim the reward because acceptance requires knowledge of the offer at the time of performance
questions.e: Lalman Shukla (1913) holds that there can be no acceptance without knowledge of the offer; performing the requested act in ignorance of the reward creates no contract.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 148 defines bailment as delivery of goods for a purpose on condition of return; Section 151 requires the bailee to take as much care as a person of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods. A leaves his car with B for servicing; B parks it unlocked on the street and it is stolen. Under the stated principle:
o: B is not liable because theft is beyond his control
Bailment imposes no duty of care
B is liable only if he stole the car himself
B is liable for failing to exercise the ordinary-prudence standard of care required of a bailee under Section 151
questions.e: Section 151 imposes on the bailee the duty to take the care that a person of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods of similar bulk and value; parking unlocked on the street breaches that standard.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 126 defines a contract of guarantee among creditor, principal debtor and surety; Section 128 makes the surety's liability co-extensive with the principal debtor's unless otherwise agreed. A guarantees B's loan from a bank; B defaults. The bank sues A without first suing B. A objects. Under the stated principle:
o: A's objection succeeds because the creditor must exhaust remedies against the principal debtor first
The bank can proceed directly against A because the surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor's under Section 128
Guarantees are enforceable only after the debtor's insolvency
A surety is liable only for half the debt
questions.e: Section 128 makes the surety liable co-extensively with the principal debtor, so the creditor may proceed against the surety without first suing the principal debtor, unless the contract provides otherwise.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 182 defines an agent as one employed to do acts for another; Section 196 permits ratification, by which the principal adopts an unauthorised act with retrospective effect. A's employee, without authority, buys raw material on A's behalf; A later sells the material at a profit, knowing the facts. Under the stated principle:
o: A is not bound because the employee lacked authority
An employer can never ratify an employee's act
A has ratified the purchase under Section 196 by accepting its benefit with knowledge, binding himself retrospectively
questions.e: Section 196 allows ratification where the principal, with full knowledge, adopts the unauthorised act; accepting and dealing with the goods manifests ratification, relating back to the date of the act.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 15 defines coercion as committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code, or unlawful detention of property, to compel consent. A threatens to file a false criminal case against B unless B sells his land cheaply; B agrees. Under the stated principle:
o: The sale is valid because B signed voluntarily
The agreement is voidable at B's option because consent was obtained by coercion under Sections 15 and 19
Threats of legal action can never be coercion
Only physical force amounts to coercion
questions.e: Threatening a false criminal prosecution to extract consent is coercion under Section 15; under Section 19, an agreement induced by coercion is voidable at the option of the aggrieved party.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 16 defines undue influence where one party dominates the will of another and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage; Section 19A makes such contracts voidable. A spiritual guru induces his devotee to gift valuable property for blessings. The devotee challenges the gift. Under the stated principle:
o: The gift stands because religious gifts are always valid
Undue influence requires a written threat
The gift is voidable because the guru's dominant position over the devotee raises a presumption of undue influence under Section 16
questions.e: Section 16(2) presumes undue influence where a person in a position of real or apparent authority — such as a spiritual adviser over a devotee — obtains an advantage; the transaction is voidable under Section 19A unless shown to be fair.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 17 defines fraud as false suggestion, active concealment, or promise made without intention to perform. A sells a house knowing its foundation is cracked, actively concealing the defect from B. Under the stated principle:
o: B has no remedy because buyers must inspect
Concealment is fraud only if in writing
The contract is voidable for fraud under Sections 17 and 19 because of active concealment of a material defect
Fraud requires a criminal conviction first
questions.e: Active concealment of a material fact by one having knowledge of it is fraud under Section 17(2); a contract induced by fraud is voidable at the option of the deceived party under Section 19.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 20 voids agreements where both parties are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement. A agrees to buy B's horse, and both A and B believe the horse to be a thoroughbred racehorse; it is in fact an ordinary horse with no racing pedigree. Under the stated principle:
o: The contract is valid because both parties agreed on the sale
The agreement is void under Section 20 because both parties shared a mistake as to a fact essential to the agreement
The buyer must pay the full price
questions.e: Section 20 renders void an agreement where both parties labour under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement; the shared false assumption about the horse's essential character (racehorse versus ordinary horse) destroys true consent.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 30 declares agreements by way of wager void, and no suit lies to recover winnings. In Gherulal Parakh v. Mahadeodas (1959), the Court distinguished wagering from speculative commercial contracts. A and B bet ₹1,00,000 on a cricket match outcome; A wins and sues B for the money. Under the stated principle:
o: A's suit fails because wagering agreements are void under Section 30
A can recover because bets are enforceable
A can recover if the bet was in writing
Wagering is a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment
questions.e: Section 30 makes wagering agreements void and bars suits for recovery of winnings; a pure bet on an uncertain event with no other interest is the classic wager.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 124 defines indemnity as a promise to save another from loss caused by the promisor or a third person. An insurance contract is the classic example. A promises to indemnify B against losses from a business venture. Loss occurs through a third party's default. A refuses to pay. Under the stated principle:
o: A is liable under the contract of indemnity in Section 124, which expressly covers loss caused by the promisor's own conduct or that of any other person
A need not pay because the loss was caused by a third party
Indemnity covers only the promisor's own acts
Insurance contracts are not indemnity contracts
questions.e: Section 124 defines indemnity to include loss caused by the conduct of the promisor or of any other person; the indemnifier must make good losses within the promise's scope regardless of who caused them.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 70 covers obligations where a person lawfully does something for another not intending to act gratuitously, and the other enjoys the benefit — the latter must compensate. A, a contractor, mistakenly delivers construction material to B's site; B uses it knowing of the mistake. Under the stated principle:
o: B must compensate A under Section 70 because he accepted the benefit of a non-gratuitous act
B need not pay because there was no contract
Section 70 applies only to government contracts
questions.e: Section 70 (quasi-contract) obliges a person who enjoys the benefit of a non-gratuitous act to compensate the doer, even absent a formal contract, preventing unjust enrichment.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 62 provides that if parties agree to substitute a new contract or rescind or alter the original, the original need not be performed — novation. A owes B ₹5,00,000; A, B and C agree that C will pay B and A is discharged. B later sues A. Under the stated principle:
o: B can still sue A because the original debt survives
B's suit against A fails because novation under Section 62 discharged A's original obligation
questions.e: Section 62 provides that a valid novation substituting a new contract discharges the original contract; once A, B and C agreed to substitute C's obligation, A's liability ended.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 4 of the Indian Contract Act provides that communication of acceptance is complete as against the proposer when it is put in the course of transmission to him (for example, when posted), and Section 5 allows revocation of a proposal only before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer. A offers to sell his car to B; B posts a letter of acceptance; before the letter reaches A, A telephones B revoking the offer. Under the stated principle:
o: A's revocation is ineffective because B's acceptance was complete against A when the letter was posted, and a proposal cannot be revoked thereafter
A's revocation is effective because it reached B before the acceptance letter reached A
Revocation by telephone is always effective
The contract is complete only when A acknowledges the letter
questions.e: Under Sections 4–5, acceptance is complete against the proposer the moment it is posted; a proposal may be revoked only before that point. A's later telephonic revocation is therefore ineffective, and a binding contract arose on posting.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 37 requires parties to perform their promises; Section 39 provides that refusal to perform entitles the other party to terminate. A contracts to build a house for B; halfway through, A abandons the work declaring he will not return. Under the stated principle, B may:
o: Only wait indefinitely for A to return
Sue only after the original completion date
Treat the contract as at an end under Section 39 and claim damages, because anticipatory breach entitles the promisee to terminate
Recover nothing because the house is incomplete
questions.e: Section 39 codifies anticipatory breach: when one party refuses to perform, the promisee may put an end to the contract and claim compensation without waiting for the due date of performance.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: A contingent contract under Section 31 depends on the happening of an uncertain future event; Section 32 enforces it only if the event happens. A agrees to pay B ₹2,00,000 if A's ship returns safely; the ship sinks. Under the stated principle:
o: A must pay because he promised
A need not pay because the contingent event did not happen, so under Section 32 the contract cannot be enforced
B can claim half the amount
questions.e: Section 32 provides that contingent contracts to do or not do something if an uncertain future event happens cannot be enforced unless and until that event has happened.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 72 requires repayment of money paid by mistake or under coercion. A pays B ₹50,000 mistakenly believing he owes it, though no debt exists. B refuses to refund. Under the stated principle:
o: B may keep the money because A paid voluntarily
Mistake of fact never grounds recovery
B must refund under Section 72 because money paid under a mistake of fact is recoverable
A must prove fraud to recover
questions.e: Section 72 (quasi-contract) obliges a person to repay money paid by mistake or under coercion; even a voluntary payment under a mistaken belief of liability is recoverable.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: In Balfour v. Balfour (1919), the Court held domestic arrangements between spouses lack intention to create legal relations. Applied in India in Raj Rani v. Prem Adib (1949), A promises his wife a monthly allowance during a harmonious marriage with no business context. She sues when he stops. Under the stated principle:
o: Her claim fails because purely domestic arrangements are presumed to lack intention to create legal relations
She wins because all promises are contracts
Spouses can never contract with each other
The claim succeeds if the amount is large
questions.e: Following Balfour v. Balfour as applied in India, agreements between spouses in a domestic context are presumed not to intend legal relations, an essential element of a contract under Section 10.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: In Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932), Lord Atkin laid down the neighbour principle: a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer. A buys a sealed bottle of juice manufactured by B; the juice is contaminated and A falls ill. B argues he owes a duty only to the retailer who bought from him. Under the stated principle:
o: B is right because privity exists only with the retailer
Manufacturers are never liable in tort
A must sue the retailer only
B owes a duty of care to A as the ultimate consumer under the neighbour principle, and breach causing foreseeable harm is actionable negligence
questions.e: Donoghue v. Stevenson established that manufacturers owe a duty of care to ultimate consumers of their products; absence of a direct contractual relationship does not defeat a negligence claim for foreseeable harm.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) imposes strict liability where a person brings onto his land something likely to cause mischief if it escapes, for a non-natural use of land. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987, Oleum gas leak), the Supreme Court laid down absolute liability for hazardous industries, without the Rylands exceptions. A chemical factory's toxic gas escapes injuring neighbours; the factory pleads an unforeseeable equipment failure. Under the stated principle:
o: The factory escapes liability because the failure was unforeseeable
Strict liability applies but the act-of-God exception saves the factory
The factory is absolutely liable under M.C. Mehta because enterprises engaged in hazardous activities owe an absolute duty with no exceptions
Only the government can be liable for gas leaks
questions.e: M.C. Mehta (1987) replaced Rylands strict liability with absolute liability for hazardous industries in India: the enterprise is liable for harm from its hazardous activity without any exceptions such as act of God or third-party acts.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The maxim volenti non fit injuria bars recovery where the plaintiff voluntarily assumes a known risk. A spectator attends a cricket match, sits in an unscreened area near the boundary despite warnings, and is hit by a six. He sues the organisers. Under the stated principle, the most likely outcome is:
o: He recovers because organisers must guarantee safety
His claim fails under volenti non fit injuria because he knowingly accepted the obvious risk of the sport
questions.e: Volenti non fit injuria defeats a claim where the plaintiff, with full knowledge of the risk, voluntarily encounters it; watching cricket from an exposed area is a classic assumed risk of the sport.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Vicarious liability makes an employer liable for torts committed by an employee in the course of employment. A delivery driver, while on his delivery route, negligently injures a pedestrian. The employer claims the driver alone is liable. Under the stated principle:
o: The employer is vicariously liable because the negligence occurred in the course of the driver's employment
The employer is right because only the wrongdoer pays
Vicarious liability applies only to intentional torts
Employers are liable only if they ordered the negligence
questions.e: Under respondeat superior, an employer is liable for employees' torts committed within the course of employment; a delivery driver negligently driving on his route squarely falls within that scope.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: In Kasturilal v. State of U.P. (1965), the Supreme Court held the State immune for torts committed in the exercise of sovereign functions. Later, in Nagendra Rao v. State of A.P. (1994), the Court narrowed this immunity. A police officer, while seizing smuggled gold in a statutory raid (sovereign function), negligently loses the gold. The owner sues the State. Under the stated principle, the older position holds:
o: The State is liable in all cases of employee negligence
Sovereign immunity was abolished in India
The officer's negligence converts the act to non-sovereign
Under Kasturilal, the State is immune because the seizure was in exercise of a sovereign function
questions.e: Kasturilal drew the sovereign/non-sovereign distinction, immunising the State for torts in exercise of sovereign functions like police seizure of contraband; though later narrowed, it remains the classical statement of the doctrine.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Defamation requires a false statement published to a third party that lowers the claimant in the estimation of right-thinking people. Truth and fair comment are defences. A newspaper falsely reports that a businessman was convicted of fraud, though he was acquitted. He sues. Under the stated principle:
o: The newspaper is protected because news is privileged
Public figures cannot sue for defamation
The businessman can recover because a false published statement lowering his reputation is defamatory, and truth is not available as a defence
questions.e: A false published imputation of criminal conviction lowers reputation in the eyes of right-thinking members of society and is actionable; the defence of truth fails where the statement is false.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Nuisance is unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of land. A factory emits noxious fumes day and night, making a neighbour's house uninhabitable. The factory argues it provides local employment. Under the stated principle:
o: The factory's economic utility defeats the claim
Nuisance requires physical damage to property
Only the State can sue for nuisance
The neighbour can obtain an injunction and damages because substantial, continuous interference with enjoyment of property is an actionable private nuisance
questions.e: Private nuisance protects the use and enjoyment of land; continuous noxious emissions rendering a home uninhabitable are actionable regardless of the defendant's economic utility, with injunction as the primary remedy.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Res ipsa loquitur allows negligence to be inferred where the accident is of a kind that ordinarily does not occur without negligence and the instrumentality was in the defendant's control. A pedestrian is hit by a barrel falling from a warehouse window. Under the stated principle:
o: The pedestrian must produce an eyewitness to the negligence
The maxim applies only to medical negligence
Res ipsa loquitur applies: barrels do not ordinarily fall from windows without negligence, shifting the evidential burden to the warehouse owner
Falling objects can never prove negligence
questions.e: Res ipsa loquitur permits an inference of negligence where the thing causing harm was under the defendant's management and the accident is of a type that ordinarily bespeaks negligence, as in the classic Byrne v. Boadle barrel case.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines 'deficiency' in Section 2(11) and provides a three-tier redressal system. After the 2021 amendment, pecuniary jurisdiction is: District Commissions up to ₹50 lakh, State Commissions ₹50 lakh–₹2 crore, National Commission above ₹2 crore. A consumer who paid ₹75 lakh as consideration for the goods complains of deficiency. Under the stated principle, it lies before:
questions.e: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (as amended in 2021), pecuniary jurisdiction is determined by the value of consideration paid: District Commissions up to ₹50 lakh, State Commissions ₹50 lakh–₹2 crore, and the National Commission above ₹2 crore. A ₹75 lakh consideration places the complaint before the State Commission.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Sections 82–87 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 introduce product liability: manufacturers, service providers and sellers may be liable for harm caused by defective products. A pressure cooker with a manufacturing defect explodes injuring a consumer. Under the stated principle:
o: The manufacturer is liable under the product liability provisions for harm caused by the manufacturing defect
Product liability requires proof of negligence
Consumers cannot claim for personal injury
questions.e: The 2019 Act's product liability chapter imposes liability on the product manufacturer for harm caused by a manufacturing defect, without requiring the consumer to prove negligence.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Injuria sine damno means violation of a legal right without actual damage, actionable per se, as in Ashby v. White (1703) where a voter wrongfully prevented from voting recovered though his candidate won. A is wrongfully prevented by an officer from casting his vote; his candidate wins anyway. Under the stated principle:
o: A cannot sue because he suffered no loss
A can sue because injuria sine damno — infringement of the legal right to vote — is actionable without proof of damage
Voting rights are not legal rights
Only candidates can sue for electoral wrongs
questions.e: Ashby v. White established that where a legal right is infringed, the law presumes damage; injuria sine damno is actionable per se without proof of actual loss.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Damnum sine injuria means actual loss without violation of a legal right, which is not actionable, as in Mogul Steamship v. McGregor (1892) where lawful competition causing loss was held not actionable. A opens a lawful shop next to B's shop; B loses customers. Under the stated principle:
o: B can sue for loss of business
B can sue if his losses are large
B cannot sue because lawful competition causing economic loss is damnum sine injuria — loss without legal injury
questions.e: Mogul Steamship holds that loss caused by lawful competition violates no legal right and is damnum sine injuria, which the law does not remedy.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The remoteness rule in The Wagon Mound (1961) holds a defendant liable only for damage of a kind reasonably foreseeable. A negligently spills a small quantity of oil in a harbour; the oil unforeseeably ignites, burning ships. Under the stated principle, liability for the fire damage depends on:
o: Whether the defendant intended the fire
The size of the oil spill
Whether fire damage from spilt oil was reasonably foreseeable — if not, it is too remote
questions.e: The Wagon Mound replaced the directness test of Re Polemis with reasonable foreseeability: a defendant is liable only for damage of a kind that a reasonable person would have foreseen as a consequence of the negligence.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: False imprisonment is total restraint of liberty without lawful justification, as in Bird v. Jones (1845) where partial obstruction was held insufficient. Police detain A for six hours without arrest, warrant or legal authority. Under the stated principle:
o: No tort is committed because A was not handcuffed
A can sue for false imprisonment because complete restraint without lawful authority violates personal liberty
Detention under six hours is always lawful
Only the State can commit false imprisonment
questions.e: False imprisonment requires total restraint of movement without lawful justification; unauthorised police detention, however brief, satisfies both elements and is actionable.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Contributory negligence in India is treated as comparative: damages are apportioned by relative fault, as recognised in cases like Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Laxman Iyer (2003). A pedestrian crossing against the signal is hit by a speeding driver; the court finds the pedestrian 30% at fault. Under the stated principle:
o: Damages are reduced proportionately — the pedestrian recovers 70% — because contributory negligence merely reduces, not defeats, the claim
Contributory negligence is a complete defence in India
questions.e: Indian courts apply comparative fault for contributory negligence: the claimant's damages are reduced in proportion to his share of responsibility rather than being wholly defeated.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Private defence is a complete defence in tort where reasonable force is used to protect person or property. A thief enters B's house at night; B uses moderate force to restrain him until police arrive. The thief sues for battery. Under the stated principle:
o: The thief recovers because any force is battery
Private defence applies only to public property
B's claim of private defence succeeds because reasonable force to protect person and property against a wrongdoer is justified
questions.e: The law permits reasonable force in defence of person and property; restraining an intruder with moderate force until police arrive is proportionate and defeats a battery claim.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Malicious prosecution requires: prosecution by the defendant, termination in the claimant's favour, absence of reasonable cause, and malice. A rival businessman engineers a baseless criminal complaint against B to ruin him; B is acquitted. Under the stated principle, B's suit for malicious prosecution:
o: Succeeds if B proves the prosecution was initiated without reasonable cause and with malice, ending in his favour
Fails because acquittal alone is insufficient
Fails because business rivalry is lawful
questions.e: Malicious prosecution requires all four elements — institution of proceedings, favourable termination, lack of reasonable and probable cause, and malice; a rival's baseless complaint to destroy a competitor satisfies them when proved.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Assault is an act creating reasonable apprehension of imminent harmful contact; battery is the actual infliction of force. A raises a stick threatening to hit B, who flinches, but A does not strike. Under the stated principle:
o: No tort is committed without physical contact
A commits assault because his act created reasonable apprehension of imminent battery, though no battery occurred
questions.e: Assault is complete when the defendant's act intentionally causes reasonable apprehension of imminent harmful or offensive contact; actual contact (battery) is a separate tort and not required.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Nervous shock is compensable where psychiatric injury is a foreseeable result of negligence, as developed from Dulieu v. White (1901). A mother witnesses her child being negligently run over due to a driver's fault and suffers recognised psychiatric illness. Under the stated principle:
o: She cannot recover because she was not physically injured
She can recover for psychiatric injury as a primary victim's close relative where such injury was foreseeable
questions.e: Courts allow recovery for negligently inflicted psychiatric injury where it is a foreseeable consequence to a person of ordinary fortitude in the claimant's position, particularly close relatives witnessing the event.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 as amended in 2019 provides no-fault liability under Section 164: ₹5,00,000 for death and ₹2,50,000 for grievous hurt, regardless of the wrongdoer's fault. A pedestrian is killed by a vehicle; the driver claims the pedestrian was at fault. Under the stated principle:
o: The claim fails because the pedestrian was at fault
The legal representatives are entitled to ₹5,00,000 under Section 164 without proving the driver's fault
questions.e: Section 164 of the amended Motor Vehicles Act imposes no-fault liability: fixed compensation is payable for death or grievous hurt in a motor accident without the claimant proving negligence or wrongful act.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Passing off protects goodwill against misrepresentation causing confusion, even without a registered trademark. A sells soft drinks as 'Coca-Kola' in similar packaging, confusing consumers. Under the stated principle:
o: No action lies without trademark registration
The original manufacturer can sue for passing off because misrepresentation likely to confuse consumers and damage goodwill is actionable
Only the government can stop imitation
questions.e: Passing off is a common-law economic tort protecting goodwill: selling goods under a confusingly similar get-up that misleads consumers is actionable without any registered trademark.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) under Section 10 of the 2019 Act can act against misleading advertisements; Section 89 punishes false or misleading advertisements with imprisonment up to two years and fine. A company runs ads falsely claiming its cream cures baldness. Under the stated principle:
o: No action lies because advertising is free speech
Only consumers who bought the cream can complain
The CCPA can order discontinuation and penalties because misleading advertisements are punishable under the 2019 Act
Misleading ads are regulated only by the ASCI code
questions.e: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 empowers the CCPA to act against misleading advertisements: Section 89 prescribes imprisonment up to two years and fine for a manufacturer or service provider causing a false or misleading advertisement, while Section 21 lets the CCPA impose penalties up to ₹10 lakh on the manufacturer or endorser and bar an endorser from endorsements.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Trespass to land is actionable per se without proof of damage. A repeatedly walks across B's fenced farm despite warnings, causing no physical damage. Under the stated principle:
o: B can sue because trespass to land is actionable per se — unauthorised entry itself violates the right to exclusive possession
B cannot sue because no damage occurred
Walking across land is never trespass
questions.e: Trespass to land protects the right to exclusive possession and is actionable per se; unauthorised entry, even without causing damage, entitles the possessor to sue.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Ex turpi causa non oritur actio bars claims founded on the claimant's own illegal act. Two burglars quarrel over division of stolen goods; one sues the other for his 'share'. Under the stated principle:
o: The court will divide the loot fairly
The thief can recover if he was the victim
Ex turpi causa applies only to contracts
The claim fails because courts will not assist a claimant whose case is founded on his own illegal act
questions.e: Ex turpi causa prevents a claimant from founding an action on his own illegality; courts refuse to adjudicate division of the proceeds of crime.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: In Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das (2000), the Supreme Court awarded compensation against the Railways for rape committed by railway employees in a railway building, holding the State vicariously liable for constitutional torts. A woman is assaulted by on-duty railway staff in a railway retiring room. Under the stated principle:
o: The Railways are not liable because rape is a personal act
The Railways are vicariously liable and must compensate because the assault by employees in the course of their duties violates fundamental rights
Only the individual employees are liable
Constitutional torts do not exist in Indian law
questions.e: Chandrima Das established that the State is vicariously liable to compensate victims of fundamental-rights violations by its employees acting in the course of employment, extending tort liability into public law.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Article 50 of the Constitution directs the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive. This directive principle was given effect notably through:
o: The creation of the Election Commission
The separation achieved via the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, which divided judicial and executive magistrates
questions.e: Article 50's mandate to separate the judiciary from the executive was substantially implemented by the CrPC, 1973, which created distinct cadres of Judicial Magistrates and Executive Magistrates, ending the colonial system of executive officers trying criminal cases.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The pardoning power of the President — to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions and commutations in cases of court-martial, Union law offences and death sentences — is conferred by:
questions.e: Article 72 confers the President's clemency power covering court-martial cases, offences against Union laws, and death sentences; Article 161 gives Governors a narrower parallel power excluding court-martial cases.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Article 74(1), as amended by the 42nd Amendment, provides that the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers. In Samsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974), the Supreme Court held that:
o: The President and Governor are bound to act on ministerial advice except in the narrow areas where the Constitution permits discretion
The President may act in his discretion in all matters
Ministers serve at the President's pleasure without advice
questions.e: Samsher Singh (1974) held that the President (and Governor) exercise their powers on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, with discretion available only where the Constitution expressly or by necessary implication permits it.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The Attorney-General for India, the Government of India's first law officer, is appointed under Article 76. A person qualified to be appointed must:
o: Have served as a High Court judge for ten years
Be qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court
questions.e: Article 76(1) requires the Attorney-General to be qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court — that is, a citizen with the prescribed standing at the Bar or judicial office.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Article 108 provides for a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament to resolve deadlocks on a Bill (other than a Money Bill or constitutional amendment Bill), presided over by:
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
questions.e: Article 118 (read with Article 108) provides that a joint sitting summoned by the President is presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, or in his absence, the Deputy Speaker.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The President's power to promulgate Ordinances when Parliament is not in session is contained in Article 123. In D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987), dealing with the Governor's parallel power, the Supreme Court held that:
o: The President may legislate permanently through ordinances
Repromulgation of ordinances repeatedly without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution
Ordinances require prior Supreme Court approval
questions.e: D.C. Wadhwa (1987) condemned the mechanical repromulgation of ordinances (Bihar had repromulgated some over 200 times) as a colourable exercise and fraud on the Constitution, since the ordinance power is meant for emergent situations.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Article 141 declares that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within India. This makes Supreme Court decisions:
o: Binding precedent on all courts in India, including High Courts and subordinate courts
Binding only on the parties to the case
questions.e: Article 141 gives the Supreme Court's declared law the status of binding precedent throughout the territory of India; all courts below it must follow the ratio decidendi.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in any pending cause or matter. In practice, this extraordinary power has been used for:
o: Granting relief beyond ordinary law to secure complete justice, such as in the Bhopal gas tragedy settlement and Ayodhya mediation contexts
questions.e: Article 142 confers a unique power to do complete justice, used sparingly to mould relief beyond strict legal entitlements — famously in the Bhopal settlement (Union Carbide v. Union of India, 1989) — though it cannot override express statutory prohibitions.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In Ismail Faruqui v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court dealt with the Article 143 Presidential Reference on the acquisition of the Ayodhya area by:
o: Answering the reference on whether a Hindu temple had pre-existed at the site
Declining to answer the reference while upholding the Acquisition of Certain Area at Ayodhya Act, 1993
Striking down the acquisition as violative of secularism
Transferring the reference to the Allahabad High Court
questions.e: In Ismail Faruqui (1994) the majority upheld the 1993 acquisition Act but declined to answer the Presidential Reference, treating the question whether a temple had pre-existed as vague and unnecessary; the Court also observed that a mosque is not an essential part of Islam for Article 25 purposes.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, the guardian of the public purse who audits Union and State accounts, is provided for in:
questions.e: Article 148 establishes the office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General, appointed by the President with security of tenure similar to a Supreme Court judge, removable only like a judge.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Article 226 empowers every High Court to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose. Compared with Article 32, the High Court's writ jurisdiction is:
o: Wider in scope ('any other purpose') but discretionary, whereas the Article 32 remedy is itself a fundamental right
Narrower, because it covers only fundamental rights
Available only against the Union government
questions.e: Article 226 extends to any other purpose beyond fundamental rights, making it wider in subject matter than Article 32; however, unlike Article 32, it is discretionary and the right to move the High Court is not itself a fundamental right.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Article 249 empowers Parliament to legislate on State List subjects in the national interest if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. Such a resolution remains in force for:
questions.e: Under Article 249(2), a Rajya Sabha resolution authorising Parliament to legislate on a State subject in the national interest lasts one year and may be renewed annually by fresh resolutions.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: The Finance Commission, which recommends the distribution of tax revenues between the Union and States, is constituted by the President every five years under:
questions.e: Article 280 mandates the President to constitute a Finance Commission every five years (or earlier) to recommend tax-sharing, grants-in-aid, and measures to augment State resources.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down clauses (4) and (5) inserted into Article 368 by the 42nd Amendment and held that:
o: Directive principles override fundamental rights in all cases
The basic structure doctrine was overruled
Harmony between fundamental rights and directive principles is part of the basic structure, and a limited amending power is itself a basic feature
questions.e: Minerva Mills (1980) held that the balance between Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure and that clauses seeking to make Parliament's amending power unlimited destroy the Constitution's essential identity.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-judge bench held regarding laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 that:
o: They are completely immune from judicial review
They remain subject to basic structure review, including fundamental rights forming part of the basic structure
Only pre-1973 laws can be challenged
questions.e: I.R. Coelho (2007) held that Ninth Schedule insertions after Kesavananda's date (24 April 1973) are not immunised from judicial review and must survive the basic structure test.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997), the Supreme Court laid down:
o: Eleven mandatory requirements for arrest and detention, including preparation of a memo of arrest and informing a friend or relative
questions.e: D.K. Basu (1997) issued eleven binding requirements to be followed in all cases of arrest and detention — arrest memo, inspection memo, informing relatives, medical examination — enforceable through contempt and compensation.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In Lalita Kumari v. Government of U.P. (2014), the Supreme Court held that:
o: Registration of an FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC (now Section 173 BNSS) when information discloses a cognizable offence
Police have discretion whether to register FIRs
Preliminary enquiry is mandatory in all cases
FIRs can only be registered with a magistrate's permission
questions.e: Lalita Kumari (2014) held FIR registration mandatory on disclosure of a cognizable offence, allowing preliminary enquiry only in limited categories like matrimonial or commercial disputes.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court:
o: Upheld Section 66A of the IT Act
Struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 as vague and overbroad, violating Article 19(1)(a)
questions.e: Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A for vagueness and overbreadth, holding it chilled free speech; the Court distinguished discussion and advocacy (protected) from incitement (unprotected).

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court:
o: Struck down Section 497 IPC criminalising adultery as violative of Articles 14, 15 and 21, treating the wife as the husband's property
Upheld adultery as a criminal offence
Held adultery is only a civil wrong with no remedy
questions.e: Joseph Shine (2018) unanimously struck down Section 497 IPC, holding it perpetuated the notion of women as chattel and violated equality, non-discrimination and dignity; adultery remains a ground for divorce.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which:
o: Disqualified all candidates with criminal cases
Gave convicted legislators a three-month window to appeal while retaining their seats
questions.e: Lily Thomas (2013) struck down Section 8(4), which had allowed convicted MPs/MLAs to continue for three months pending appeal; disqualification now takes effect immediately on conviction for the listed offences.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court held regarding daughters' coparcenary rights under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act (as amended in 2005) that:
o: Daughters get coparcenary rights only if the father was alive in 2005
The 2005 amendment is prospective only for married daughters
Coparcenary rights are available only to sons
Daughters acquire coparcenary rights by birth, irrespective of whether the father was alive on 9 September 2005
questions.e: Vineeta Sharma (2020) clarified that daughters become coparceners by birth under the amended Section 6, regardless of the father's survival on the amendment's commencement date, partially overruling Prakash v. Phulavati (2016).

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014), the Supreme Court directed that in offences punishable with imprisonment up to seven years, police must:
o: Issue a notice of appearance under Section 41A CrPC (now Section 35 BNSS) and record reasons for arrest, with magistrates verifying compliance
questions.e: Arnesh Kumar (2014) made Section 41A notices mandatory before arrest in offences carrying up to seven years' imprisonment and required magistrates to verify compliance, targeting routine, unjustified arrests.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024), a seven-judge bench held that:
o: Sub-classification of Scheduled Castes for reservation is unconstitutional
States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes for reservation to extend benefits to the most disadvantaged, overruling E.V. Chinnaiah (2005)
Only the Union may classify castes
questions.e: Davinder Singh (2024) overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2005) and held that States can sub-classify SCs to give preferential treatment within reservation to the weakest sections, provided the classification is based on empirical data.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 permits divorce by mutual consent after the parties have lived separately for one year; the statute prescribes a six-month waiting period between the first and second motions. In Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017), the Supreme Court held the six-month period is directory, not mandatory. A couple seeks waiver of the waiting period after settling all issues. Under the stated principle:
o: The court must always insist on the full six months
The court may waive the six-month cooling period where the statutory conditions are satisfied and there is no chance of reconciliation
Mutual consent divorce requires three years of separation
The waiting period can be waived only by the High Court
questions.e: Amardeep Singh (2017) held the six-month period in Section 13B(2) is directory; courts may waive it where the parties have genuinely settled, the waiting period's purpose stands fulfilled, and no useful purpose would be served by delay.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), a 3:2 majority struck down instantaneous triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) as unconstitutional. Parliament then enacted the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019. Under the 2019 Act, pronouncement of instant triple talaq is:
o: Void, illegal, and punishable with imprisonment up to three years
questions.e: The 2019 Act declares talaq-e-biddat void and illegal and makes its pronouncement a cognizable, non-bailable offence punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, giving statutory teeth to Shayara Bano.

questions.subject: Legal reasoning
questions.q: Passage: Section 125 CrPC (now Section 144 BNSS) provides maintenance to wives, children and parents unable to maintain themselves. In Shah Bano (1985), the Supreme Court held a divorced Muslim woman could claim maintenance under Section 125. In Shabana Bano v. Imran Khan (2010), the Court clarified that:
