Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) — narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping without consent violate Articles 20(3) and 21.
State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961) — giving handwriting or thumb impressions is not ‘being a witness’ under Article 20(3).
Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kishanrao Gorantyal (2020) — a Section 65B certificate is mandatory for admitting electronic records.
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) — struck down Section 66A of the IT Act for chilling free speech.
Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) — freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) includes the right to access the internet.
Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950) — freedom of the press flows from Article 19(1)(a).
Sakal Papers v. Union of India (1962) — struck down the Newspaper (Price and Page) Act as violating press freedom.
Bennett Coleman v. Union of India (1972) — the newsprint policy case protecting press freedom.
R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (1994) — the Auto Shankar case balancing press freedom with the right to privacy.
Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) — triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) declared unconstitutional.
Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) — decriminalised consensual same-sex relations by reading down Section 377 IPC.
Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) — struck down adultery as a criminal offence under Section 497 IPC.
Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018) — the Sabarimala verdict; women of all ages may enter the temple.
NALSA v. Union of India (2014) — recognised transgender persons as a third gender with equal rights.
The basic structure doctrine holds that Parliament’s amending power cannot destroy the Constitution’s essential features (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).

The doctrine of eclipse holds that a pre-constitutional law inconsistent with fundamental rights is eclipsed, not dead, and revives if the inconsistency is removed (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 1955).
The doctrine of severability holds that only the unconstitutional part of a law is struck down while the rest survives (Article 13; R.M.D.C. v. Union of India, 1957).
The doctrine of waiver holds that fundamental rights cannot be waived by an individual (Basheshar Nath v. CIT, 1959).
The doctrine of pith and substance holds that a law’s true nature decides which legislative list it falls under (State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, 1951).
The doctrine of colourable legislation holds that a legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa, 1953).
The doctrine of territorial nexus allows a state law to operate outside the state where there is a sufficient territorial connection (Wallace Brothers v. CIT, 1948).

The doctrine of repugnancy holds that under Article 254, a state law repugnant to a parliamentary law on the Concurrent List is void to the extent of the repugnancy (M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India, 1979).
The doctrine of harmonious construction requires provisions of the Constitution to be read together so all are given effect (In re: Kerala Education Bill, 1957).
The doctrine of prospective overruling lets a court declare the law for the future without unsettling past transactions; first used in Golaknath (1967).
The doctrine of promissory estoppel binds the government to its promise where a citizen has acted upon it (Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of Uttar Pradesh, 1979).
The doctrine of legitimate expectation requires administrative action to be fair where a citizen reasonably expects a benefit (Food Corporation of India v. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed, 1993).
The doctrine of proportionality requires state action to be no more restrictive than necessary to achieve its object (Om Kumar v. Union of India, 2001).
Wednesbury unreasonableness strikes down a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it (Associated Provincial Picture Houses v. Wednesbury Corporation, 1948).
The public trust doctrine holds that the State holds natural resources as a trustee for the public (M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath, 1997).
The doctrine of parens patriae treats the State as guardian of those unable to protect themselves; invoked in the Bhopal gas tragedy case (Charan Lal Sahu v. Union of India, 1989).
The doctrine of sovereign immunity shields the State from liability for sovereign functions (Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of Uttar Pradesh, 1965).
The rule of absolute liability imposes liability without exceptions on hazardous industries; laid down after the Oleum gas leak (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, 1987).
The rule of strict liability imposes liability without fault when a dangerous thing escapes one’s land (Rylands v. Fletcher, 1868).
The doctrine of frustration makes a contract void when its performance turns impossible (Section 56, Indian Contract Act; Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur, 1954).
The indoor management rule (Turquand rule) lets outsiders assume a company’s internal procedures were properly followed (Royal British Bank v. Turquand, 1856).
The rule in Foss v. Harbottle (1843) holds that the company, not individual shareholders, is the proper plaintiff for wrongs done to it.
The doctrine of lis pendens bars transfer of disputed property during pending litigation so the decree is not defeated (Section 52, Transfer of Property Act).
The doctrine of part performance protects a transferee in possession under an unregistered contract against the transferor (Section 53A, Transfer of Property Act).
The rule against perpetuity forbids tying up property beyond lives in being plus eighteen years (Section 14, Transfer of Property Act).
The first Law Commission was set up in 1834 with Lord Macaulay as chairman; it drafted the Indian Penal Code.
Harilal J. Kania was the first Chief Justice of India, serving from 1950 to 1951.
Justice Fathima Beevi became the first woman judge of the Supreme Court in 1989.
Justice Y.V. Chandrachud is the longest-serving Chief Justice of India, from February 1978 to July 1985.
Justice K.N. Singh had the shortest tenure as Chief Justice of India — just eighteen days in 1991.
India has not yet had a woman Chief Justice of India.
The Supreme Court of India was established on 28 January 1950, succeeding the Federal Court of India set up in 1937.
The High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, established in 1862, are India’s oldest High Courts.
India has twenty-five High Courts; the newest is the Telangana High Court, established in 2019.
The National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) was constituted in 1995 under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
The first Lok Adalat was held on 14 March 1982 at Junagadh in Gujarat.
A Lok Adalat award is deemed a decree of a civil court, and no appeal lies against it.
The Bar Council of India was established in 1961 under the Advocates Act, 1961.
B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly, while B.N. Rau served as its Constitutional Adviser.
BNS in force from 1 July 2024, replacing the IPC 1860 — 358 sections in 20 chapters.
BNSS in force from 1 July 2024, replacing the CrPC 1973 — 531 sections.
BSA in force from 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Evidence Act 1872 — 170 sections.
BNS Section 100 defines culpable homicide (IPC 299); Section 101 defines murder (IPC 300); Section 103 punishes murder (IPC 302).
BNS Section 80 is dowry death (IPC 304B); Sections 85-86 cover cruelty (IPC 498A).
BNS Section 137 is kidnapping (IPC 359-361) and Section 138 is abduction (IPC 362).
BNS Section 303 is theft (IPC 378); its proviso allows community service for first-time petty theft below Rs 5,000 with return of the value.
BNS Section 318 is cheating (IPC 415); Section 336 is forgery (IPC 463).
BNS Section 356 is defamation (IPC 499), retaining the ten exceptions including truth for the public good.
BNS Section 351 is criminal intimidation (IPC 503); Sections 115-116 are hurt and grievous hurt (IPC 319-320).
BNS Section 152 punishes acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India — the recast successor to sedition, with IPC 124A omitted.
BNS Section 111 creates the offence of organised crime; Section 113 defines a terrorist act.
BNS Section 103(2) punishes murder by a mob of five or more on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language or personal belief.
BNS Section 304 creates the standalone offence of snatching.
BNS Section 69 punishes sexual intercourse by deceitful means, including a false promise of marriage.
BNS Section 62 punishes attempt (IPC 511).
BNSS Section 173 governs the FIR, including Zero FIR and e-FIR by electronic communication.
BNSS Section 35 carries the Arnesh Kumar safeguards: notice of appearance where arrest is not required, recorded reasons where it is (CrPC 41A).
BNSS Section 187: police remand 90 days for offences punishable with death, life or 10+ years, 60 days otherwise; 15 days' police custody may be split.
BNSS Sections 283-288 cover summary trials; Section 285 caps imprisonment after summary trial at three months.
BNSS Section 356 permits trial and judgment in the absence of a proclaimed person.
BNSS Section 530 allows proceedings in electronic mode; Section 258(1) requires a Sessions judgment within 30 days of completion of arguments, extendable to 45 days for recorded reasons.
BNSS Section 531 is the savings clause: pending trials and investigations continue under the repealed CrPC.
BSA Section 23 covers confessions (IEA 25-27); Section 26 covers dying declarations (IEA 32); Section 39 covers expert opinion (IEA 45).
BSA Section 63 needs a certificate for electronic records (IEA 65B); Section 118 raises the dowry-death presumption (IEA 113B); Section 109 covers facts especially within knowledge (IEA 106).
Article 142 lets the Supreme Court pass any order needed for complete justice — invoked for Priyanka Saxena's IAF re-induction in September 2026.
Article 143 lets the President seek the Supreme Court's advisory opinion; in Ismail Faruqui (1994) the Court declined to answer the Ayodhya reference.
The 1st Amendment (1951) added Articles 31A and 31B, the Ninth Schedule and Article 15(4) — provoked by Champakam Dorairajan (SC) and Kameshwar Singh (Patna HC).
The 24th Amendment (1971) declared Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution — the answer to Golaknath.
The 42nd Amendment (1976), the 'Mini-Constitution', added socialist, secular and integrity to the Preamble and inserted the fundamental duties.
The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from Article 31, made it Article 300A, and made Article 21 non-suspendable during Emergency.
The 52nd Amendment (1985) inserted the Tenth Schedule — the anti-defection law.
The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to Panchayats and municipalities — Parts IX and IXA.
The 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A: free and compulsory education for ages 6-14.
The 97th Amendment (2011) gave constitutional status to cooperative societies — Part IXB.
The 101st Amendment (2016) brought the GST — Articles 246A, 269A and the GST Council under 279A.
The 103rd Amendment (2019) gave 10% EWS reservation — Articles 15(6) and 16(6), upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022).
The 104th Amendment (2020) extended SC/ST seat reservation and ended Anglo-Indian nominated seats.
The 105th Amendment (2021) restored the states' power to identify socially and educationally backward classes.
The 106th Amendment (2023), the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserves 33% of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and assemblies after delimitation.
Article 32 is the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution (Ambedkar) — the SC's writ power for fundamental rights.
Article 226 gives High Courts wider writ powers than Article 32 — for any purpose, not only fundamental rights.
Article 51A lists the eleven fundamental duties — added by the 42nd Amendment and not directly enforceable by courts.
Article 141 makes Supreme Court law binding on all courts; Article 144 obliges authorities to act in its aid.
The Seventh Schedule divides subjects into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists under Article 246.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Parliament cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.
Maneka Gandhi (1978): Article 21 procedure must be fair, just and reasonable.
Minerva Mills (1980): harmony between fundamental rights and directive principles; limited amending power.
S.R. Bommai (1994): secularism is part of the basic structure; Article 356 proclamations face judicial review.
Vishaka (1997): guidelines against workplace sexual harassment — the parent of the 2013 Act.
Lily Thomas (2013): struck down Section 8(4) of the RP Act — convicted legislators stand disqualified at once.
The NJAC case (2015): the 99th Amendment fell 4:1 and the collegium system survived.
Shayara Bano (2017): triple talaq held unconstitutional by 3:2.
Puttaswamy (2017): privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21.
Navtej Johar (2018): consensual same-sex relations decriminalised under Section 377 IPC.
Joseph Shine (2018): adultery under Section 497 IPC struck down.
The Ayodhya verdict (2019): unanimous 5-0 — the disputed site for a Ram temple trust, five acres for a mosque.
Anuradha Bhasin (2020): internet access is part of Article 19; indefinite Section 144 orders are unconstitutional.
Janhit Abhiyan (2022): the EWS quota upheld 3:2.
TPA Section 6(a): a spes successionis — an heir's mere chance of succeeding — cannot be transferred.
TPA Section 14 states the rule against perpetuity: vesting beyond lives in being plus 18 years is void.
TPA Section 41 protects a bona fide transferee who buys from an ostensible owner.
TPA Section 52 is lis pendens: a buyer during pending litigation is bound by the decree.
TPA Section 53A shields part performance only if the contract is registered — the 2001 amendment made registration compulsory.
TPA Section 54: sale of tangible immovable property worth Rs 100 or more needs a registered instrument.
TPA Section 60 gives the mortgagor the right of redemption; no clog may be put on it.
TPA Section 106: after the 2002 amendment, a 15-day notice to quit need not expire with the end of the tenancy month.
TPA Section 123: gifts of immovable property must be made by registered instrument.
Suraj Lamp (2011): sale-agreement, GPA and will transactions do not convey title — only a registered deed does.
The 2013 land acquisition Act needs 70% consent for PPP and 80% for private projects, with compensation at twice urban and four times rural market value.
Indore Development Authority (2020): acquisition lapses under Section 24(2) only if the state neither took possession nor paid compensation.
Hindu Succession Act Section 14 turns a widow's limited estate into absolute ownership.
Shah Bano (1985) led to the Muslim Women Act 1986; Danial Latifi (2001) read in a reasonable and fair provision for the divorced wife.
Sarla Mudgal (1995): a second marriage after conversion, without divorcing the first wife, is bigamy.
Salomon v. Salomon (1897): a company is a legal person separate from its members.
The Turquand rule (1856): outsiders dealing bona fide with a company may assume indoor formalities were complied with.
Derry v. Peek (1889): deceit needs knowledge of falsity — the fraud standard for prospectus claims.
Companies Act Section 135: CSR at 2% of average net profits of the last three financial years.
Companies Act Sections 241-244: oppression and mismanagement relief needs 100 members or one-tenth of the membership, whichever is less.
Wednesbury (1948): a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could make it is unlawful.
Motilal Padampat (1979): promissory estoppel can bind the government to its representation.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997): tribunal decisions face High Court scrutiny under Articles 226-227; judicial review is basic structure.
Article 300A: no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law — a constitutional right, not a fundamental right.
The Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Act 2026 comes into force on 1 October 2026; registration delayed beyond two years needs a Judicial Magistrate First Class order.

In September 2026 the Supreme Court collegium approved the proposal to appoint 12 additional judges as permanent judges in the Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Uttarakhand and Gauhati High Courts (formal appointment follows by Presidential warrant).
The Delhi High Court's Senior Advocate Rules, notified 3 September 2026, replaced the 100-point system with full-court consensus or a two-thirds vote.

The Supreme Court on 27 May 2026 upheld only the ECI's original 24 June 2025 SIR order; the ECI stated in September 2026 that later SIR schedules had the unanimous approval of all three Election Commissioners, with SIR completed in 20 States and UTs.
In September 2026 the Supreme Court held fair investigation to be a constitutional right under Article 21 while ordering a de novo SIT probe in the Dharmasthala case.
In September 2026 the Supreme Court ordered residential premises used for commercial activity to be sealed, warning authorities against pick-and-choose enforcement.
In September 2026 the Calcutta High Court quashed the EPFO's pro-rata circular for higher pension — the third High Court to reject it.
The Supreme Court's Advocate-on-Record examination for December 2026 is scheduled for 19, 20, 22 and 23 December 2026, for qualifying re-appearance candidates.
The Places of Worship Act 1991 bars conversion of places of worship and freezes their religious character as on 15 August 1947, excluding Ayodhya.
In September 2026 the Supreme Court revised the Noida DM's plea without staying the quashing of the student's NSA detention — only the strictures and Rs 5 lakh costs were paused.
Tenth Schedule paragraph 2(1)(a): voluntarily giving up party membership disqualifies a legislator — applied to Danam Nagender by the Telangana High Court in September 2026.
Hindu Marriage Act Section 13B governs mutual-consent divorce; Amardeep Singh (2017) lets courts waive the six-month cooling period.
Contract Act Section 56: a contract becomes void when performance turns impossible — the doctrine of frustration.
The Limitation Act gives 3 years for most suits and 12 years for suits for possession of immovable property.
Order VII Rule 11 CPC lets a court reject a plaint disclosing no cause of action or barred by law.
BNSS Section 163 carries the old Section 144 CrPC power to issue urgent orders in cases of nuisance or apprehended danger.
Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression; reasonable restrictions are listed in Article 19(2).

oneliners.subject: Judiciary
oneliners.text: The Supreme Court issued notice to the Centre and the Election Commission on 13 Oct 2026 on a PIL challenging blanket immunity to the CEC and ECs.

oneliners.subject: Culture
oneliners.text: HAL, the National Culture Fund and the Archaeological Survey of India signed an MoA for conservation and development of heritage sites (13 Oct 2026).

oneliners.subject: Judiciary
oneliners.text: The Supreme Court agreed to hear Asaduddin Owaisi’s plea against the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls with other pending petitions (October 2026).

oneliners.subject: Current Affairs
oneliners.text: CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were sent to 5-day judicial custody in Tihar Jail for allegedly trespassing at Delhi's Jantar Mantar during an SIR protest (Oct 2026).

oneliners.subject: Current Affairs
oneliners.text: Bar Council of Delhi announced new office-bearers with Nitin Ahlawat elected Chairman (Oct 2026).

oneliners.subject: Constitution
oneliners.text: The MHA clarified on 15 Oct 2026 that the Home Secretary's 'unconditional apology' before the Supreme Court in a contempt matter was procedural — every affidavit responding to a contempt notice must begin with an unconditional apology.

oneliners.subject: Constitution
oneliners.text: CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke is free to hold the 'Tiranga March' at Connaught Place on 16 Oct 2026; the SC asked the government to clarify the de-notification of Jantar Mantar as a protest site.

oneliners.subject: Constitution
oneliners.text: M.K. Stalin urged the TVK government to file an appeal in the Supreme Court over reservation for converted Muslims, after the SC's 15 Oct 2026 ruling on conversion and quota benefits.

oneliners.subject: Current Affairs
oneliners.text: On 15 October 2026 the Supreme Court considered a panel headed by a retired woman judge over 'very serious' molestation allegations against police during the Delhi protests, and granted protection to a woman journalist booked under the SC/ST Act.

oneliners.subject: Judiciary
oneliners.text: The Supreme Court published draft Regulations for Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Courts, 2026, in June 2026, including provisions to verify AI-generated output and hold parties accountable for hallucinations.

oneliners.subject: Judiciary
oneliners.text: The Yes Bank AT-1 bonds judgment (15 October 2026) is 2026 INSC 1132; the GST/IBC limitation judgment (14 October 2026) is 2026 INSC 1121.

oneliners.subject: CLAT
oneliners.text: CLAT 2027: registration at consortiumofnlus.ac.in closed 31 October 2026; admit cards expected in the third/fourth week of November 2026 — Verified: 17 Oct 2026

oneliners.subject: Judiciary
oneliners.text: SC on 17 October 2026: internet access is a fundamental right under Articles 21 and 19(1)(a), extending to children (Justices Pardiwala and Chandran).

oneliners.subject: Judiciary
oneliners.text: SC on 15 October 2026 (2026 INSC 1132): Rs 8,415 crore Yes Bank AT-1 write-down set aside; action must stay within statute and scheme.

oneliners.subject: Judiciary
oneliners.text: SC on 16 October 2026: private complaints allowed for false election affidavits under Section 125A, RoP Act; Section 195 CrPC no bar.

oneliners.subject: Judiciary
oneliners.text: SC on 9 October 2026 (2026 INSC 1105): direct recruits rank above compassionate appointees in seniority.

oneliners.subject: Current Affairs
oneliners.text: CLAT 2027 registration closes on 31 October 2026 at 11:59 PM at consortiumofnlus.ac.in; the exam is on 6 December 2026 (2-4 PM, offline).

oneliners.subject: Current Affairs
oneliners.text: CLAT 2027 offers about 4,092 UG and 1,599 PG seats across 26 NLUs and IIULER Goa; over 92,000 candidates are expected.

oneliners.subject: Current Affairs
oneliners.text: CLAT 2027 fee: Rs 4,000 (General/OBC) and Rs 3,500 (SC/ST/BPL/PwD); UG eligibility 45% in Class 12 (40% for SC/ST); PG eligibility 50% in LLB (45% for SC/ST).

oneliners.subject: Current Affairs
oneliners.text: Supreme Court of India: 130 Junior Court Attendant posts (Advt F.3/2026-SC (RC), dated 15 October 2026) - online applications 4-25 November 2026 on sci.gov.in; Class 10 pass (maximum Class 12), age 18-27 as on 1 October 2026; fee Rs 1,500 (Rs 750 for reserved categories).

oneliners.subject: Current Affairs
oneliners.text: Supreme Court of India: 65 Senior Personal Assistant posts (Advt F.6/11/SPA/2026-SC (RC), dated 12 October 2026) - online applications 20 October-10 November 2026; degree plus English shorthand 110 w.p.m. and computer typing 40 w.p.m.; age 18-30; Level 8 pay (Rs 47,600-1,51,100).

oneliners.subject: CLAT
oneliners.text: CLAT 2027 fixed for 6 December 2026 (2-4 PM); applications open until 31 October 2026 on consortiumofnlus.ac.in. (21 Oct 2026)

oneliners.subject: Current Affairs
oneliners.text: NIRF 2025 law rankings: NLSIU Bangalore No. 1, NLU Delhi No. 2, NLU Kolkata No. 4. (21 Oct 2026)

oneliners.subject: Constitutional Law
oneliners.text: 15 Oct 2026: SC described the internet as a “marketplace of ideas” — Article 19(1)(a) covers the right to know, receive and impart information and ideas.

oneliners.subject: Legal GK
oneliners.text: 22 Oct 2026: CLAT 2027 notification released 15 Oct 2026 — registration closes 31 Oct 2026; exam 6 Dec 2026; 24 NLUs; fee ₹4,000 general / ₹3,500 SC/ST/BPL.

oneliners.subject: Legal GK
oneliners.text: 22 Oct 2026: AILET 2027 (NLU Delhi) — apply by 10 Nov 2026; exam 13 Dec 2026; 150 questions, 70 on Logical Reasoning.

oneliners.text: 23 Oct 2026: Supreme Court of India: 250 Junior Court Assistant posts (last date 28 Oct 2026); 65 Senior Personal Assistant (10 Nov 2026); 20 Court Master (15 Nov 2026).

oneliners.text: 23 Oct 2026: Italy enacted Legislative Decree No. 179 implementing the EU Artificial Intelligence Act — AgID and ACN enforcement; fines up to EUR 35 million or 7% of global turnover; regulatory sandbox for enterprises.

oneliners.text: 23 Oct 2026: ICAI CA Final November 2026 admit cards released at eservices.icai.org; Group I: 2, 4, 6 Nov; Group II: 9, 11, 13 Nov.

alerts.title: CLAT 2027 registration closes 31 October
alerts.body: Apply by 31 October for the 6 December exam. The correction window opens around 2 November and the admit card is expected around 25 November.

alerts.title: CLAT test cities removed: Vellore & Tiruvarur
alerts.body: Vellore and Tiruvarur have been removed from the CLAT 2027 test-city list. If you chose either city, log in and change your city preference by 31 October — otherwise the consortium will allot a city for you.
